topics.name: Limits and Continuity
topics.description: Explore how limits formalize the idea of approaching a value. Master limit evaluation techniques, continuity, the Squeeze Theorem, and the Intermediate Value Theorem.

concepts.title: Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?
concepts.content_html:
Can Change Occur at an Instant?

Imagine you're driving and glance at your speedometer. It reads 60 mph. But what does that mean? You haven't traveled 60 miles — you've only looked at the speedometer for an instant. How can we measure speed at a single moment in time?

This question — can change occur at an instant? — is the motivating idea behind calculus.

Average vs. Instantaneous Rate of Change

We know how to compute average speed: divide the total distance by the total time.

\[\text{Average speed} = \frac{\Delta \text{distance}}{\Delta \text{time}} = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\]

But instantaneous speed asks: what happens as the time interval shrinks to zero? That is, what is the speed at a single instant?

Calculus answers this by introducing the concept of a limit — we look at what the average rate of change approaches as the interval becomes infinitely small.

The Big Idea

The entire field of calculus rests on this insight:

Key Idea: By examining what happens as quantities get closer and closer to a target value (without necessarily reaching it), we can define and compute instantaneous rates of change, areas, and other quantities that seem impossible to measure directly.

What You'll Learn in This Course

AP Calculus AB covers three major ideas:

  1. Limits — the mathematical tool that makes calculus rigorous
  2. Derivatives — instantaneous rates of change (Unit 2—5)
  3. Integrals — accumulation of change and area (Unit 6—8)

All of these are built on limits, which is why we start here.

problems.question_html: A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. What is its average speed?

hints.text: Average speed = total distance divided by total time.
Compute \(\frac{150}{3}\).

problems.question_html: A ball's height (in feet) at time \(t\) seconds is given by \(h(t) = -16t^2 + 64t\). What is the average rate of change of height from \(t = 1\) to \(t = 3\)?

hints.text: Average rate of change \(= \frac{h(3) - h(1)}{3 - 1}\).

solution_steps.text: Average rate of change \(= \frac{48 - 48}{3 - 1} = \frac{0}{2} = 0\) ft/s. The ball is at the same height at both times (going up then coming down).

problems.question_html: What is the average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x = 2\) to \(x = 5\)?
What is the average rate of change of \(f(x) = 3x + 1\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 10\)?

hints.text: For a linear function \(f(x) = mx + b\), the average rate of change over any interval is always the slope \(m\).

solution_steps.text: This equals the slope of the line, which makes sense — a linear function has a constant rate of change.

problems.question_html: A particle moves along a line so that its position at time \(t\) seconds is \(s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t\) meters. The average velocity from \(t = 1\) to \(t = 1 + h\) is computed for several values of \(h\). As \(h \to 0\), this average velocity approaches a value. What does that value represent?

choices.text: The total distance traveled from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\)

hints.text: The average velocity over \([1, 1+h]\) is \(\frac{s(1+h) - s(1)}{h}\). What does this ratio approach as \(h \to 0\)?
As the time interval shrinks to zero, the average rate of change becomes the instantaneous rate of change  --  the instantaneous velocity.

solution_steps.text: The average velocity over \([1, 1+h]\) is \(\frac{s(1+h) - s(1)}{h}\).
As \(h \to 0\), this difference quotient approaches the derivative \(s'(1)\), which is the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 1\).

problems.question_html: The temperature \(T\) (in °F) of a cup of coffee at time \(t\) minutes is given by \(T(t) = 70 + 130e^{-0.05t}\). The average rate of change of \(T\) from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 10\) is approximately \(-4.79\) °F/min. Which statement best interprets this value?

choices.text: The coffee cools by exactly 4.79 °F every minute for the first 10 minutes
On average, the coffee's temperature decreases by about 4.79 °F per minute over the first 10 minutes
The instantaneous rate of cooling at \(t = 5\) is \(-4.79\) °F/min

hints.text: An average rate of change gives the overall rate across the entire interval, not the rate at any particular instant.
The negative sign means the temperature is decreasing. The average rate is the total change divided by the total time.

solution_steps.text: The average rate of change \(\frac{T(10) - T(0)}{10 - 0} \approx -4.79\) °F/min.
This means that, on average, the temperature decreases by about 4.79 °F per minute over the first 10 minutes. It does not mean the rate is constant  --  the cooling rate changes over time.

problems.question_html:
A car's position is given by \(s(t) = 2t^2 + 3t\) feet, where \(t\) is in seconds.

(a) Find the average velocity from \(t = 2\) to \(t = 2 + h\) in terms of \(h\).

(b) Simplify your expression and determine what it approaches as \(h \to 0\).

(c) Interpret your answer in context.
problems.sample_answer: The average velocity is (2(2+h)^2 + 3(2+h) - 14)/h = (4h + 2h^2 + 3h)/h = 2h + 7. As h approaches 0, the average velocity approaches 11 ft/s, which is the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.
rubric: Correctly computes s(2) = 14 and s(2+h) = 2(2+h)^2 + 3(2+h)
Simplifies average velocity to 2h + 7 (or equivalent)
Correctly evaluates the limit as h→0 to get 11 ft/s and interprets it as instantaneous velocity

hints.text: Average velocity = \(\frac{s(2+h) - s(2)}{h}\). First compute \(s(2) = 2(4) + 3(2) = 14\).

solution_steps.text: As \(h \to 0\), the average velocity approaches \(11\) ft/s. This is the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 2\): the car is traveling at 11 ft/s at that moment.

problems.correct_answer: The average velocity is (2(2+h)^2 + 3(2+h) - 14)/h = (4h + 2h^2 + 3h)/h = 2h + 7. As h approaches 0, the average velocity approaches 11 ft/s, which is the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.

problems.question_html:
A rock is dropped from a 400-foot cliff. Its height at time \(t\) seconds is \(h(t) = 400 - 16t^2\).

(a) Find the average velocity from \(t = 3\) to \(t = 3.1\), from \(t = 3\) to \(t = 3.01\), and from \(t = 3\) to \(t = 3.001\).

(b) Based on your calculations, estimate the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\).

(c) What does the sign of your answer tell you about the rock's motion?
problems.sample_answer: Average velocities: -97.6, -96.16, -96.016 ft/s. The instantaneous velocity at t=3 is -96 ft/s. The negative sign indicates the rock is falling (height is decreasing).
rubric: Correctly computes at least two average velocities approaching -96
Estimates instantaneous velocity as -96 ft/s
Interprets the negative sign as downward motion (height decreasing)

hints.text: Average velocity = \(\frac{h(3 + \Delta t) - h(3)}{\Delta t}\). Compute \(h(3) = 400 - 16(9) = 256\) first.

solution_steps.text: The average velocities approach \(-96\) ft/s, so the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\) is \(-96\) ft/s. The negative sign means the rock is falling  --  its height is decreasing at 96 ft/s.

problems.correct_answer: Average velocities: -97.6, -96.16, -96.016 ft/s. The instantaneous velocity at t=3 is -96 ft/s. The negative sign indicates the rock is falling (height is decreasing).

concepts.title: Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation
concepts.content_html:
What Is a Limit?

A limit describes the value that a function approaches as its input approaches a particular number. We write:

\[\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\]

This is read: "the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\) is \(L\)."

Important Distinction

The limit is about what \(f(x)\) approaches, not necessarily what \(f(a)\) equals. The function doesn't even need to be defined at \(x = a\) for the limit to exist.

One-Sided Limits

Sometimes we need to consider what happens from just one direction:

  • Left-hand limit: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)\) — approaching \(a\) from values less than \(a\)
  • Right-hand limit: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)\) — approaching \(a\) from values greater than \(a\)
Key Fact: The two-sided limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) exists if and only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal:
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L\)

When Limits Don't Exist

A limit does not exist (DNE) if:

  • The left-hand and right-hand limits are different
  • The function oscillates without settling near any value
  • The function increases or decreases without bound (we say the limit is \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\), which technically means DNE as a finite limit)

Example

Consider \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}\). At \(x = 1\), the function is undefined (division by zero). But:

\[\frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} = \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = x + 1 \quad \text{for } x \neq 1\]

As \(x \to 1\), \(x + 1 \to 2\). So \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} = 2\), even though \(f(1)\) is undefined.
concepts.content_raw: Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation

problems.question_html: If \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = 5\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = 5\), what is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\)?

hints.text: If both one-sided limits exist and are equal, then the two-sided limit equals that common value.
Both one-sided limits equal 5, so the two-sided limit is 5.

solution_steps.text: Since \(\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = 5\), the two-sided limit exists and equals 5.

problems.question_html: If \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^-} g(x) = 4\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^+} g(x) = 7\), what is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} g(x)\)?

hints.text: For the two-sided limit to exist, the left-hand and right-hand limits must be equal.
Since \(4 \neq 7\), the two-sided limit does not exist.

solution_steps.text: The left-hand limit is 4 and the right-hand limit is 7.
Since \(4 \neq 7\), the two-sided limit \(\lim_{x \to 2} g(x)\) does not exist.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{x^2 - 16}{x - 4}\).

hints.text: Factor the numerator: \(x^2 - 16 = (x-4)(x+4)\).
Cancel the \((x-4)\) factor and substitute \(x = 4\).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -1} \frac{x^2 + 3x + 2}{x + 1}\).

hints.text: Factor the numerator: \(x^2 + 3x + 2 = (x+1)(x+2)\).
Cancel the \((x+1)\) factor. The limit becomes \(\lim_{x \to -1}(x+2)\).

problems.question_html: Consider the function \(f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1 & \text{if } x < 3 \\ 10 & \text{if } x = 3 \\ 5x - 8 & \text{if } x > 3 \end{cases}\). What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\)?

hints.text: The limit depends on the values \(f(x)\) approaches as \(x \to 3\), not the value \(f(3)\).
From the left: \(2(3) + 1 = 7\). From the right: \(5(3) - 8 = 7\). Both sides agree, so the limit is 7.

solution_steps.text: Since both one-sided limits equal 7, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 7\). Note that \(f(3) = 10\), but this does not affect the limit.

problems.question_html: Which of the following must be true if \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} g(x) = 12\)?

hints.text: A limit existing at a point does not require the function to be defined or continuous there.
A two-sided limit equals \(L\) if and only if both one-sided limits equal \(L\).

solution_steps.text: If \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} g(x) = 12\), then by definition both \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5^-} g(x) = 12\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5^+} g(x) = 12\).
The function need not be defined at \(x = 5\), and even if it is, \(g(5)\) need not equal 12. Continuity also is not guaranteed.

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & \text{if } x < 1 \\ 2 & \text{if } x = 1 \\ 3 - x & \text{if } x > 1 \end{cases}\).

(a) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x)\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x)\).

(b) Does \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\) exist? Explain.

(c) Does \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = f(1)\)? What does this tell you about continuity?
problems.sample_answer: Left-hand limit = 1, right-hand limit = 2. The two-sided limit does not exist because the one-sided limits are not equal. Since the limit DNE, continuity fails at x = 1.
rubric: Correctly computes left-hand limit as 1 and right-hand limit as 2
States the two-sided limit does not exist because the one-sided limits differ
Explains that continuity fails because the limit does not exist (or does not equal f(1))

hints.text: For each one-sided limit, use the corresponding piece of the piecewise function.
From the left: \(x^2 \to 1\). From the right: \(3 - x \to 2\). These are not equal.

solution_steps.text: Since \(1 \neq 2\), the one-sided limits are not equal, so \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\) does not exist.
Because the limit does not exist at \(x = 1\), the function is not continuous at \(x = 1\) regardless of the value \(f(1) = 2\). This is a jump discontinuity.

problems.correct_answer: Left-hand limit = 1, right-hand limit = 2. The two-sided limit does not exist because the one-sided limits are not equal. Since the limit DNE, continuity fails at x = 1.

problems.question_html:
A function \(g\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4^-} g(x) = 7\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4^+} g(x) = 7\), but \(g(4) = 3\).

(a) What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)\)?

(b) Is \(g\) continuous at \(x = 4\)? Justify using the definition of continuity.
problems.sample_answer: The two-sided limit is 7 since both one-sided limits equal 7. The function is NOT continuous at x = 4 because the limit (7) does not equal f(4) = 3.
rubric: States the two-sided limit is 7
Identifies the function is not continuous at x = 4
Justifies by citing the condition lim f(x) = f(a) fails since 7 ≠ 3

hints.text: Both one-sided limits are equal, so the two-sided limit exists.
Continuity at \(x = 4\) requires three things: \(g(4)\) exists, \(\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)\) exists, and they are equal.

solution_steps.text: Since \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4^-} g(x) = \lim_{x \to 4^+} g(x) = 7\), we have \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} g(x) = 7\).
For continuity at \(x = 4\), we need: (1) \(g(4)\) is defined ✓ (it equals 3), (2) \(\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)\) exists ✓ (it equals 7), (3) \(\lim_{x \to 4} g(x) = g(4)\) ✗ (since \(7 \neq 3\)).
Condition (3) fails, so \(g\) is not continuous at \(x = 4\). This is a removable discontinuity.

problems.correct_answer: The two-sided limit is 7 since both one-sided limits equal 7. The function is NOT continuous at x = 4 because the limit (7) does not equal f(4) = 3.

concepts.title: Estimating Limit Values from Graphs
concepts.content_html:
Reading Limits from Graphs

One of the most common ways limits appear on the AP exam is through graphs. You'll be given the graph of a function and asked to determine various limits.

How to Read \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) from a Graph

  1. Approach from the left: Trace the curve from the left side toward \(x = a\). What \(y\)-value does the curve approach? That's \(\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)\).
  2. Approach from the right: Trace the curve from the right side toward \(x = a\). What \(y\)-value does the curve approach? That's \(\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)\).
  3. Compare: If both one-sided limits are equal, the two-sided limit equals that value. If they differ, the two-sided limit DNE.

Common Graph Features

  • Hole (removable discontinuity): Open circle at \((a, L)\). The limit exists and equals \(L\), but \(f(a) \neq L\) (or is undefined).
  • Jump discontinuity: The curve approaches different values from left and right. The two-sided limit DNE.
  • Vertical asymptote: The curve shoots off to \(\pm\infty\). The limit is \(\pm\infty\) (or DNE as a finite number).
AP Exam Tip: Always check the one-sided limits separately. Many students lose points by only looking at one side of the graph. Also remember: the value \(f(a)\) (solid dot) is irrelevant to the limit — only the behavior near \(a\) matters.

Limits at Specific Points

When a graph shows a filled circle (solid dot) at a point, that's the actual function value \(f(a)\). When it shows an open circle, the function is either undefined there or defined at a different value. The limit depends only on where the curve is heading, not on the dot.

problems.question_html: A graph of \(f(x)\) shows: as \(x\) approaches 3 from the left, the curve approaches \(y = 5\); as \(x\) approaches 3 from the right, the curve approaches \(y = 5\); and there is an open circle at \((3, 5)\) with a solid dot at \((3, 2)\). What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\)?

hints.text: The limit depends on where the curve approaches, not on the actual function value (solid dot).
Both sides approach \(y = 5\), so the limit is 5. The fact that \(f(3) = 2\) does not affect the limit.

solution_steps.text: Since both one-sided limits are equal, \(\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 5\).
Note: \(f(3) = 2\) (the solid dot), but the limit is 5 — the limit and function value can differ.

problems.question_html: A graph of \(g(x)\) shows the curve approaching \(y = 1\) as \(x \to 4^-\) and approaching \(y = 3\) as \(x \to 4^+\). What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)\)?

hints.text: For the two-sided limit to exist, both one-sided limits must be equal.
Since \(1 \neq 3\), the two-sided limit does not exist.

solution_steps.text: Since \(1 \neq 3\), \(\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)\) does not exist (jump discontinuity).

problems.question_html: A graph shows \(f(x)\) with a vertical asymptote at \(x = 2\). As \(x \to 2^-\), the graph goes to \(+\infty\). As \(x \to 2^+\), the graph goes to \(+\infty\). What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\)?

hints.text: When both one-sided limits go to \(+\infty\), we write \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \infty\).
Even though the limit is \(\infty\), technically this means the limit does not exist as a finite number. However, we write \(\infty\) to describe the behavior.

solution_steps.text: We write \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \infty\). This describes the unbounded behavior, even though the limit technically DNE as a finite value.

problems.question_html: From a graph, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = 4\) and \(f(1) = 4\). However, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) = 4\) as well. Is \(f\) continuous at \(x = 1\)?

choices.text: No, because there is a hole
No, because the one-sided limits differ

hints.text: Continuity requires three things: \(f(a)\) is defined, the limit exists, and they're equal.
\(f(1) = 4\), \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 4\), and both are equal — all three conditions are met.

solution_steps.text: All three conditions for continuity are satisfied, so \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).

problems.question_html: The graph of \(f\) has a hole at \((2, 5)\) and a filled dot at \((2, 3)\). What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\)?

hints.text: The limit is determined by where the graph approaches, not where the filled dot is.
The hole at \((2, 5)\) means the graph approaches \(y = 5\) from both sides. The filled dot at \((2, 3)\) is just the function value \(f(2) = 3\).

solution_steps.text: A hole (open circle) at \((2, 5)\) means the graph approaches \(y = 5\) as \(x \to 2\) from both sides.
The filled dot at \((2, 3)\) tells us \(f(2) = 3\), but the limit depends on approach behavior, not the function value.

problems.question_html: From the graph of a piecewise function \(g\), the following is observed: as \(x\) approaches \(-1\) from the left, \(g(x)\) approaches \(4\); as \(x\) approaches \(-1\) from the right, \(g(x)\) approaches \(4\); and \(g(-1) = 4\). Which statement is true?

choices.text: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -1} g(x)\) does not exist because \(g\) is piecewise
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -1} g(x) = 4\) but \(g\) is not continuous at \(x = -1\)
More information is needed to determine the limit

hints.text: Both one-sided limits equal 4, so the two-sided limit exists and equals 4.
Since the limit equals 4 and \(g(-1) = 4\), all three conditions for continuity are met.

solution_steps.text: Since \(g(-1) = 4 = \displaystyle\lim_{x \to -1} g(x)\), all three conditions for continuity are satisfied. A piecewise function can absolutely be continuous at the boundary point.

problems.question_html:
The graph of \(f\) is described as follows: for \(x < 0\), the graph follows \(y = x + 2\); for \(x > 0\), the graph follows \(y = -x + 4\); there is no point plotted at \(x = 0\).

(a) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x)\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x)\).

(b) Does \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\) exist? Explain.

(c) Sketch or describe what the graph looks like near \(x = 0\).
problems.sample_answer: Left limit = 2, right limit = 4. The two-sided limit does not exist because 2 ≠ 4. Near x = 0, the graph approaches y = 2 from the left and y = 4 from the right, creating a jump.
rubric: Correctly finds left-hand limit as 2 and right-hand limit as 4
States the two-sided limit does not exist because one-sided limits differ
Describes the graph near x = 0 as having a jump discontinuity

hints.text: Substitute \(x = 0\) into each piece: \(x + 2\) gives the left-hand limit, and \(-x + 4\) gives the right-hand limit.
Left: \(0 + 2 = 2\). Right: \(-0 + 4 = 4\). Since \(2 \neq 4\), the two-sided limit DNE.

solution_steps.text: Since \(2 \neq 4\), the two-sided limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\) does not exist.
The graph has a jump at \(x = 0\): the left branch ends at the open point \((0, 2)\) and the right branch begins at the open point \((0, 4)\), with no point plotted at \(x = 0\).

problems.correct_answer: Left limit = 2, right limit = 4. The two-sided limit does not exist because 2 ≠ 4. Near x = 0, the graph approaches y = 2 from the left and y = 4 from the right, creating a jump.

problems.question_html:
A graph of \(h(x)\) shows the following behavior near \(x = 3\): from the left, the curve increases without bound (goes to \(+\infty\)); from the right, the curve decreases without bound (goes to \(-\infty\)). There is a vertical dashed line at \(x = 3\).

(a) Write the one-sided limits using proper notation.

(b) Does \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} h(x)\) exist? Explain.

(c) What graphical feature does the vertical dashed line represent?
problems.sample_answer: lim(x→3⁻) h(x) = +∞ and lim(x→3⁺) h(x) = −∞. The two-sided limit does not exist. The vertical dashed line is a vertical asymptote.
rubric: Correctly writes both one-sided limits with proper notation and ±∞
States the two-sided limit does not exist (one-sided limits disagree or are infinite)
Identifies the vertical dashed line as a vertical asymptote at x = 3

hints.text: When a function increases or decreases without bound, we write the limit as \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\).
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^-} h(x) = +\infty\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^+} h(x) = -\infty\). Since these are not equal (and not finite), the two-sided limit DNE.

solution_steps.text: The two-sided limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} h(x)\) does not exist because the one-sided limits are not equal (and infinite limits are not finite limits).
The vertical dashed line at \(x = 3\) represents a vertical asymptote, which occurs where the function grows without bound.

problems.correct_answer: lim(x→3⁻) h(x) = +∞ and lim(x→3⁺) h(x) = −∞. The two-sided limit does not exist. The vertical dashed line is a vertical asymptote.

concepts.title: Estimating Limit Values from Tables
concepts.content_html:
Using Tables to Estimate Limits

Another common method for estimating limits is to use a table of values. We choose \(x\)-values that get progressively closer to the target value \(a\) and observe what happens to \(f(x)\).

Procedure

  1. Choose values of \(x\) approaching \(a\) from the left: e.g., \(a - 0.1\), \(a - 0.01\), \(a - 0.001\)
  2. Choose values of \(x\) approaching \(a\) from the right: e.g., \(a + 0.1\), \(a + 0.01\), \(a + 0.001\)
  3. Compute \(f(x)\) for each value
  4. Observe the pattern: if the values of \(f(x)\) are approaching the same number \(L\) from both sides, we estimate \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\)

Example

Estimate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}\) using a table:

\(x\)\(f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}\)
\(-0.1\)\(0.99833\)
\(-0.01\)\(0.99998\)
\(-0.001\)\(0.9999998\)
\(0.001\)\(0.9999998\)
\(0.01\)\(0.99998\)
\(0.1\)\(0.99833\)

The values approach 1 from both sides, so \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\).

Caution: Tables can only provide an estimate. A function could behave unexpectedly between or beyond the values you tested. Tables are useful for building intuition, but algebraic or analytic methods provide rigorous answers.

problems.question_html:
A table shows values of \(f(x)\) near \(x = 2\):

\(x\)1.91.991.9992.0012.012.1
\(f(x)\)3.83.983.9984.0024.024.2

Estimate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\).

hints.text: Look at the pattern: from the left the values approach 4, from the right they approach 4.
Since both sides approach 4, the limit is 4.

problems.question_html: A table for \(g(x)\) near \(x = 5\) shows \(g(4.9) = 10.1\), \(g(4.99) = 10.01\), \(g(5.01) = 12.01\), \(g(5.1) = 12.1\). What can you conclude about \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} g(x)\)?

hints.text: Compare the left-hand values (approaching 10) with the right-hand values (approaching 12).
Since the left-hand limit (10) \(\neq\) right-hand limit (12), the two-sided limit DNE.

problems.question_html: Using a calculator, evaluate \(f(x) = \frac{e^x - 1}{x}\) at \(x = 0.01\) and \(x = -0.01\). Based on these values, estimate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x}\).

hints.text: \(f(-0.01) \approx 0.995\). Both values are near 1.

problems.question_html: Why is a table alone not sufficient to prove the value of a limit?

choices.text: Tables only show finitely many values — the function could behave differently between tested points
Tables can only be used for polynomial functions

hints.text: Think about what a table can miss — it only samples specific \(x\)-values.

solution_steps.text: A table shows \(f(x)\) at finitely many points. The function could behave unpredictably between those points or oscillate in ways the table doesn't capture.
Tables provide estimates and build intuition, but algebraic methods are needed for rigorous proofs of limit values.

hints.text: Look at the trend of \(f(x)\) values as \(x\) gets closer to 0 from both sides.
The values approach \(2\) from both sides: \(1.9867 \to 1.99987 \to 1.999999 \to 2\).

solution_steps.text: Since both sides approach 2, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(2x)}{x} = 2\). (This can be confirmed algebraically: \(\frac{\sin(2x)}{x} = 2 \cdot \frac{\sin(2x)}{2x} \to 2 \cdot 1 = 2\).)

hints.text: Check whether the left-hand and right-hand limits agree.
From the left, \(g(x) \to 3\). From the right, \(g(x) \to 7\). Since \(3 \neq 7\), the two-sided limit DNE.

solution_steps.text: Since \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5^-} g(x) = 3 \neq 7 = \lim_{x \to 5^+} g(x)\), the two-sided limit does not exist. This indicates a jump discontinuity at \(x = 5\).

problems.question_html:
The function \(f(x) = \frac{e^x - 1 - x}{x^2}\) is undefined at \(x = 0\).

(a) Create a table of values for \(x = \pm 0.1, \pm 0.01, \pm 0.001\) and use it to estimate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\).

(b) Explain why a table alone might not be sufficient to determine a limit exactly.
problems.sample_answer: Computing f(±0.1) ≈ 0.5171, f(±0.01) ≈ 0.50017, f(±0.001) ≈ 0.500002. The limit appears to be 0.5. A table can only suggest a limit; it cannot prove convergence or detect oscillatory behavior between table values.
rubric: Correctly computes at least 3 table values showing convergence toward 0.5
Estimates the limit as 0.5 (or 1/2)
Explains a limitation of tables: they cannot prove a limit or catch oscillations between sample points

hints.text: Use a calculator to evaluate \(f(x)\) at each given \(x\)-value. Look for the pattern as \(x \to 0\).

solution_steps.text: \(f(0.001) \approx 0.500002\). By symmetry, the negative values give similar results.
The table strongly suggests \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1 - x}{x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\). (This can be confirmed using Taylor series: \(e^x = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2} + \cdots\).)
A table cannot prove a limit because it only samples finitely many points. The function could oscillate or behave unexpectedly between sample points.

problems.correct_answer: Computing f(±0.1) ≈ 0.5171, f(±0.01) ≈ 0.50017, f(±0.001) ≈ 0.500002. The limit appears to be 0.5. A table can only suggest a limit; it cannot prove convergence or detect oscillatory behavior between table values.

problems.question_html:
A student creates a table for \(h(x) = \sin\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\) near \(x = 0\):

\(x\)\(0.1\)\(0.01\)\(0.001\)\(0.0001\)
\(h(x)\)\(-0.544\)\(-0.506\)\(0.827\)\(-0.306\)

(a) Does the table suggest a limit exists? Explain.

(b) Why do the function values not settle down near a single number?
problems.sample_answer: The values do not approach any single number  --  they keep jumping around. This suggests the limit does not exist. As x→0, the argument 1/x grows without bound, causing sin(1/x) to oscillate between -1 and 1 infinitely often.
rubric: Observes that the table values do not settle toward a single number
Concludes the limit does not exist
Explains that 1/x → ∞ causes sin to oscillate infinitely without settling

hints.text: For a limit to exist, the values must approach a single number. Do these values settle down?
As \(x \to 0\), \(\frac{1}{x} \to \infty\), so \(\sin\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\) oscillates between \(-1\) and \(1\) infinitely often.

solution_steps.text: The table values jump: \(-0.544, -0.506, 0.827, -0.306\). They do not approach any single number.
As \(x \to 0^+\), \(\frac{1}{x} \to +\infty\), and \(\sin\) oscillates between \(-1\) and \(1\) infinitely rapidly.
Therefore \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \sin\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\) does not exist. This is a classic example where tabular estimation reveals oscillation that prevents a limit from existing.

problems.correct_answer: The values do not approach any single number  --  they keep jumping around. This suggests the limit does not exist. As x→0, the argument 1/x grows without bound, causing sin(1/x) to oscillate between -1 and 1 infinitely often.

concepts.title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits
concepts.content_html:
Limit Laws

When you know the limits of individual pieces, you can combine them using limit laws (also called limit properties). These let you break complex limits into simpler parts.

Suppose \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M\). Then:

Limit Laws:
1. Sum: \(\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) + g(x)] = L + M\)
2. Difference: \(\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) - g(x)] = L - M\)
3. Constant Multiple: \(\lim_{x \to a}[c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot L\)
4. Product: \(\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) \cdot g(x)] = L \cdot M\)
5. Quotient: \(\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{L}{M}\), provided \(M \neq 0\)
6. Power: \(\lim_{x \to a}[f(x)]^n = L^n\)

Direct Substitution Property

For any polynomial or rational function (where the denominator is nonzero at \(a\)), the limit equals the function value:

\[\lim_{x \to a} p(x) = p(a)\]

This is because polynomials are continuous everywhere, and rational functions are continuous wherever they're defined.

Example

Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} (3x^2 + 5x - 1)\):

By direct substitution: \(3(2)^2 + 5(2) - 1 = 12 + 10 - 1 = 21\).

No tricks needed — polynomials are continuous, so just plug in.
concepts.content_raw: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits

problems.question_html: Given that \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 4\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} g(x) = -2\), find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} [2f(x) - 3g(x)]\).

hints.text: Use the constant multiple and difference rules: \(2L - 3M\).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -1} (x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 5)\).

hints.text: This is a polynomial — use direct substitution.

problems.question_html: Given \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} f(x) = 3\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} g(x) = 7\), find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\).

hints.text: Use the quotient rule: \(\frac{L}{M}\) as long as \(M \neq 0\).
\(\frac{3}{7}\). Since \(7 \neq 0\), the quotient rule applies.

solution_steps.text: By the quotient limit law: \(\frac{\lim f(x)}{\lim g(x)} = \frac{3}{7}\)

problems.question_html: Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} \sqrt{x^2 + 9}\).

hints.text: Since the square root function is continuous for positive inputs, use direct substitution.

solution_steps.text: By the composition limit law (continuous outer function): \(\lim \sqrt{x^2+9} = \sqrt{\lim(x^2+9)}\)

problems.question_html: Given \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = -3\), find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} \bigl[4f(x) - 2g(x)\bigr]\).

hints.text: Use the constant multiple rule and the difference rule for limits.

problems.question_html: Given \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 4\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = 0\), which limit can be determined using the basic limit laws?

hints.text: The quotient law applies only when the denominator's limit is nonzero.
\(\frac{g(x)}{f(x)}\) has denominator limit \(4 \neq 0\), so the quotient law gives \(\frac{0}{4} = 0\). The others have denominator limit 0.

solution_steps.text: The quotient rule for limits states \(\displaystyle\lim \frac{f}{g} = \frac{\lim f}{\lim g}\) provided \(\lim g \neq 0\).
For \(\frac{g(x)}{f(x)}\): the denominator limit is \(4 \neq 0\), so \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{g(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{0}{4} = 0\).
The other options involve division by \(g(x)\) whose limit is 0, or \(\ln(0)\) which is undefined. The quotient law cannot be applied.

problems.question_html:
Let \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = -2\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} g(x) = 6\), and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} h(x) = 4\).

(a) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \bigl[f(x) \cdot g(x) + h(x)\bigr]\).

(b) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \sqrt{h(x) + g(x) \cdot f(x)}\).

(c) State which limit law you used in each step.
problems.sample_answer: (a) f(x)·g(x) + h(x) → (-2)(6) + 4 = -12 + 4 = -8. (b) h(x) + g(x)·f(x) → 4 + 6(-2) = -8, but sqrt(-8) is undefined, so the limit does not exist (in the reals).
rubric: Correctly applies product and sum laws to get -8 in part (a)
Identifies that the expression under the square root approaches -8 in part (b)
Concludes the limit in (b) does not exist because you cannot take the square root of a negative number

hints.text: Apply the product rule, then the sum rule. For part (b), first find the limit of the expression under the radical.
(a) \((-2)(6) + 4 = -8\). (b) The expression under \(\sqrt{}\) approaches \(-8\), so the square root is not defined for real numbers.

solution_steps.text: By the sum law: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} [f(x) \cdot g(x) + h(x)] = -12 + 4 = -8\).
Since the expression under the radical approaches \(-8 < 0\), \(\sqrt{h(x) + g(x) f(x)}\) is not real-valued near \(x = 3\), and the limit does not exist in the real numbers.

problems.correct_answer: (a) f(x)·g(x) + h(x) → (-2)(6) + 4 = -12 + 4 = -8. (b) h(x) + g(x)·f(x) → 4 + 6(-2) = -8, but sqrt(-8) is undefined, so the limit does not exist (in the reals).

problems.question_html:
Given \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 8\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} g(x) = 2\), evaluate each limit and identify the limit law used.

(a) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\)

(b) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x)]^{g(x)}\)

(c) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \bigl[3g(x)^2 - f(x)\bigr]\)
problems.sample_answer: (a) By quotient law: 8/2 = 4. (b) By the power law: 8^2 = 64. (c) By constant multiple, power, and difference laws: 3(2)^2 - 8 = 12 - 8 = 4.
rubric: Correctly applies quotient law to get 4 in part (a)
Correctly applies power law to get 64 in part (b)
Correctly applies multiple laws to get 4 in part (c)

hints.text: Use the quotient, power, constant multiple, and difference limit laws as needed.

solution_steps.text: (a) Quotient law: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim f(x)}{\lim g(x)} = \frac{8}{2} = 4\) (valid since \(\lim g(x) = 2 \neq 0\)).
(b) Power law: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x)]^{g(x)} = [\lim f(x)]^{\lim g(x)} = 8^2 = 64\) (valid since both limits are finite and the base is positive).
(c) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} [3g(x)^2 - f(x)] = 3[\lim g(x)]^2 - \lim f(x) = 3(2)^2 - 8 = 12 - 8 = 4\). Used constant multiple, power, and difference laws.

problems.correct_answer: (a) By quotient law: 8/2 = 4. (b) By the power law: 8^2 = 64. (c) By constant multiple, power, and difference laws: 3(2)^2 - 8 = 12 - 8 = 4.

concepts.title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Manipulation
concepts.content_html:
When Direct Substitution Fails

Sometimes plugging in \(x = a\) gives the indeterminate form \(\frac{0}{0}\). This doesn't mean the limit doesn't exist — it means we need to do more work.

Strategy 1: Factoring

Factor the numerator and/or denominator to cancel the common factor causing \(\frac{0}{0}\).

Example: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3} = \lim_{x \to 3}(x+3) = 6\)

Strategy 2: Conjugate Multiplication

When a radical appears, multiply by the conjugate to eliminate the radical:

Example: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+4} - 2}{x}\)

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{x+4} + 2\):

\[= \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{(x+4) - 4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} = \frac{1}{4}\]

Strategy 3: Common Denominator

When you have a complex fraction, combine terms using a common denominator:

Example: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{x+3} - \frac{1}{3}}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{3 - (x+3)}{3(x+3)}}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-x}{3x(x+3)} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-1}{3(x+3)} = -\frac{1}{9}\)

AP Exam Tip: When you get \(\frac{0}{0}\), try these strategies in order: (1) factor, (2) conjugate, (3) common denominator. If you get \(\frac{\text{nonzero}}{0}\), the limit is \(\pm\infty\) or DNE — no algebraic manipulation will help.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} \frac{x^2 - 25}{x - 5}\).

hints.text: Factor the numerator as a difference of squares.
\(x^2 - 25 = (x-5)(x+5)\). Cancel \((x-5)\) and substitute.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 9} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 3}{x - 9}\).

hints.text: Multiply by the conjugate \(\frac{\sqrt{x}+3}{\sqrt{x}+3}\).
The numerator becomes \(x - 9\), which cancels with the denominator.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(2+h)^2 - 4}{h}\).
Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{x+2} - \frac{1}{2}}{x}\).

hints.text: Combine the fractions in the numerator: common denominator is \(2(x+2)\).
Numerator becomes \(\frac{2-(x+2)}{2(x+2)} = \frac{-x}{2(x+2)}\). Now divide by \(x\).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{x^2 - 16}{x^2 - 5x + 4}\).

hints.text: Both numerator and denominator are 0 at \(x = 4\). Factor both to cancel the common factor.

solution_steps.text: Direct substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\), an indeterminate form. Factor both expressions.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 9} \frac{x - 9}{\sqrt{x} - 3}\).

hints.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(\sqrt{x} + 3\).
Or notice \(x - 9 = (\sqrt{x} - 3)(\sqrt{x} + 3)\), so the fraction simplifies to \(\sqrt{x} + 3\).

solution_steps.text: Direct substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\). Factor the numerator: \(x - 9 = (\sqrt{x} - 3)(\sqrt{x} + 3)\).

problems.question_html:
Evaluate the following limit. Show all algebraic manipulation.

\(\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{3+h} - \frac{1}{3}}{h}\)
problems.sample_answer: Combine the fractions in the numerator: [3 - (3+h)] / [3(3+h)] = -h / [3(3+h)]. Divide by h: -1/[3(3+h)]. As h→0: -1/9.
rubric: Correctly combines the complex fraction in the numerator
Simplifies to -1/[3(3+h)] after canceling h
Evaluates the limit as -1/9

hints.text: The numerator is a complex fraction. Find a common denominator for \(\frac{1}{3+h}\) and \(\frac{1}{3}\).

solution_steps.text: Note: This limit represents the derivative of \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) at \(x = 3\), which is \(-\frac{1}{9}\).

problems.correct_answer: Combine the fractions in the numerator: [3 - (3+h)] / [3(3+h)] = -h / [3(3+h)]. Divide by h: -1/[3(3+h)]. As h→0: -1/9.

problems.question_html:
Evaluate the following limit using algebraic manipulation. Show all steps.

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x + 4} - 2}{x}\)
problems.sample_answer: Multiply by conjugate: [sqrt(x+4) - 2][sqrt(x+4) + 2] / [x(sqrt(x+4) + 2)] = (x+4-4)/[x(sqrt(x+4)+2)] = x/[x(sqrt(x+4)+2)] = 1/(sqrt(x+4)+2). As x→0: 1/(2+2) = 1/4.
rubric: Multiplies by the conjugate sqrt(x+4) + 2
Simplifies numerator to x and cancels with denominator
Evaluates the limit as 1/4

hints.text: Direct substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\). Rationalize the numerator by multiplying by the conjugate.
Multiply top and bottom by \(\sqrt{x+4} + 2\). The numerator becomes \((x+4) - 4 = x\).

problems.correct_answer: Multiply by conjugate: [sqrt(x+4) - 2][sqrt(x+4) + 2] / [x(sqrt(x+4) + 2)] = (x+4-4)/[x(sqrt(x+4)+2)] = x/[x(sqrt(x+4)+2)] = 1/(sqrt(x+4)+2). As x→0: 1/(2+2) = 1/4.

concepts.title: Selecting Procedures for Determining Limits
concepts.content_html:
Choosing the Right Strategy

By now you know several techniques for evaluating limits. The key AP skill is selecting the right procedure for each problem. Here's a systematic decision process:

Step-by-Step Decision Tree

  1. Try direct substitution first. Plug in \(x = a\).
    • If you get a finite number â†' that's your answer.
    • If you get \(\frac{0}{0}\) â†' indeterminate; continue to step 2.
    • If you get \(\frac{\text{nonzero}}{0}\) â†' the limit is \(\pm\infty\) or DNE. Check the sign from each side.
  2. For \(\frac{0}{0}\): Try algebraic manipulation:
    • Can you factor? â†' Factor and cancel.
    • Is there a radical? â†' Multiply by the conjugate.
    • Complex fraction? â†' Find a common denominator.
    • Trig expression? â†' Use known trig limits or identities.
  3. Still stuck? Try a table or graph for an estimate, or consider the Squeeze Theorem (Topic 1.8).
Key Insight: The form \(\frac{0}{0}\) is not a dead end — it's a signal that the limit likely exists and algebraic work will reveal it. The form \(\frac{c}{0}\) (where \(c \neq 0\)) signals a vertical asymptote.

Known Limits You Should Memorize

These special limits appear frequently:

  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\)
  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos x}{x} = 0\)
  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} = 1\)

problems.question_html: What is the first step you should try when evaluating \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\)?

hints.text: Always start with the simplest method.
Direct substitution works for all continuous functions and tells you immediately if you need another technique.

solution_steps.text: Always try direct substitution first. If it yields a finite number, you're done.
If it yields \(\frac{0}{0}\), then move to algebraic techniques (factoring, conjugate, etc.).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(3x)}{x}\).

hints.text: Rewrite as \(3 \cdot \frac{\sin(3x)}{3x}\).
Use \(\lim_{u \to 0} \frac{\sin u}{u} = 1\) with \(u = 3x\).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2 - 5x + 6}{x^2 - 4}\).

hints.text: Direct substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\). Factor both numerator and denominator.
Numerator: \((x-2)(x-3)\). Denominator: \((x-2)(x+2)\). Cancel \((x-2)\).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 16} \frac{\sqrt{x} - 4}{x - 16}\).

hints.text: Direct substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\). Note that \(x - 16 = (\sqrt{x}-4)(\sqrt{x}+4)\).
Cancel \(\sqrt{x}-4\) to get \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+4}\).

problems.question_html: To evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}\), which technique is most appropriate?

hints.text: Try direct substitution first. If you get \(\frac{0}{0}\), look at the form of the expression.
\(x^2 - 9 = (x-3)(x+3)\), which cancels with \(x - 3\) in the denominator.

solution_steps.text: Direct substitution gives \(\frac{9 - 9}{3 - 3} = \frac{0}{0}\), an indeterminate form.
The numerator is a difference of squares: \(x^2 - 9 = (x-3)(x+3)\). Factoring and canceling \((x-3)\) yields \(x + 3\), so the limit is \(6\).

problems.question_html: Which of the following limits requires rationalizing (multiplying by a conjugate) rather than factoring?

hints.text: Rationalizing is needed when you see a radical that produces \(\frac{0}{0}\) and cannot be factored as a polynomial.
\(\frac{\sqrt{x+1} - 1}{x}\) gives \(\frac{0}{0}\) at \(x = 0\) and contains a radical, so multiplying by the conjugate \(\sqrt{x+1} + 1\) is the right approach.

solution_steps.text: Options A and C have polynomial numerators that factor easily. Option D can be solved by direct substitution (\(3(5) - 7 = 8\)).
Option B has \(\frac{\sqrt{x+1} - 1}{x}\), which gives \(\frac{0}{0}\) at \(x = 0\). The radical cannot be factored as a polynomial, so we multiply by the conjugate \(\sqrt{x+1} + 1\).

problems.question_html:
For each limit below, identify the most efficient technique and then evaluate the limit.

(a) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 5} (x^2 - 3x + 1)\)

(b) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3 - 1}{x - 1}\)

(c) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{9 + x} - 3}{x}\)
problems.sample_answer: (a) Direct substitution: 25 - 15 + 1 = 11. (b) Factor: (x-1)(x^2+x+1)/(x-1) = x^2+x+1, at x=1 gives 3. (c) Rationalize: multiply by (sqrt(9+x)+3)/(sqrt(9+x)+3), simplify to 1/(sqrt(9+x)+3), at x=0 gives 1/6.
rubric: Correctly identifies and applies direct substitution for part (a) to get 11
Correctly factors x^3 - 1 and evaluates the limit as 3 in part (b)
Correctly rationalizes and evaluates the limit as 1/6 in part (c)

hints.text: Try direct substitution first for each. If you get \(\frac{0}{0}\), decide between factoring or rationalizing based on the expression's form.
(a) No indeterminate form  --  just plug in. (b) \(x^3 - 1 = (x-1)(x^2 + x + 1)\). (c) Radical in numerator  --  use conjugate.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Direct substitution: 25 - 15 + 1 = 11. (b) Factor: (x-1)(x^2+x+1)/(x-1) = x^2+x+1, at x=1 gives 3. (c) Rationalize: multiply by (sqrt(9+x)+3)/(sqrt(9+x)+3), simplify to 1/(sqrt(9+x)+3), at x=0 gives 1/6.

problems.question_html:
A student attempts to evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2 - 4}{x^2 - 3x + 2}\) by plugging in \(x = 2\) and getting \(\frac{0}{0}\). They conclude the limit does not exist.

(a) Explain the student's error.

(b) Evaluate the limit correctly, showing your choice of procedure and all algebraic steps.
problems.sample_answer: The student's error is that 0/0 is an indeterminate form, not the value of the limit. Factor: (x-2)(x+2)/[(x-2)(x-1)] = (x+2)/(x-1). At x=2: 4/1 = 4.
rubric: Explains that 0/0 is indeterminate, not undefined  --  it means more work is needed
Factors both numerator and denominator correctly
Evaluates the limit as 4

hints.text: \(\frac{0}{0}\) is an indeterminate form  --  it means the limit might exist but requires further work.

solution_steps.text: The student's error: \(\frac{0}{0}\) is an indeterminate form, not a value. It signals that the limit may exist but requires algebraic manipulation to evaluate.

problems.correct_answer: The student's error is that 0/0 is an indeterminate form, not the value of the limit. Factor: (x-2)(x+2)/[(x-2)(x-1)] = (x+2)/(x-1). At x=2: 4/1 = 4.

concepts.title: Determining Limits Using the Squeeze Theorem
concepts.content_html:
The Squeeze Theorem

Some limits are difficult or impossible to evaluate using algebra alone. The Squeeze Theorem (also called the Sandwich Theorem) provides an elegant way to find such limits.

Squeeze Theorem: If \(g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)\) for all \(x\) near \(a\) (except possibly at \(a\) itself), and
\[\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L\]
then \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\).

The Idea

If \(f(x)\) is "squeezed" between two functions that both approach \(L\), then \(f(x)\) has no choice but to also approach \(L\).

Classic Example

Prove that \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = 0\).

We know \(-1 \le \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \le 1\) for all \(x \neq 0\).

Multiplying all parts by \(x^2\) (which is positive): \(-x^2 \le x^2\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \le x^2\)

Since \(\lim_{x \to 0}(-x^2) = 0\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 = 0\), by the Squeeze Theorem:

\[\lim_{x \to 0} x^2\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = 0\]

When to Use the Squeeze Theorem

Use it when:

  • The function involves an oscillating factor (like \(\sin\) or \(\cos\)) multiplied by something going to zero
  • Direct computation is impossible because the function oscillates infinitely
  • You can identify clear upper and lower bounds that both converge to the same limit
concepts.content_raw: Determining Limits Using the Squeeze Theorem

problems.question_html: If \(2x - 1 \le f(x) \le x^2\) for all \(x\) near \(x = 1\), what is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\)?

hints.text: Compute the limits of the bounding functions at \(x = 1\).
\(\lim(2x-1) = 1\) and \(\lim(x^2) = 1\). Both bounds approach 1.

solution_steps.text: Since both bounds have the same limit (1), by the Squeeze Theorem, \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 1\).

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x \cos\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\).

hints.text: Since \(-1 \le \cos(1/x) \le 1\), multiply by \(|x|\) to get bounds.
\(-|x| \le x\cos(1/x) \le |x|\), and both \(-|x|\) and \(|x|\) approach 0.

solution_steps.text: Since \(\lim_{x \to 0}(-|x|) = 0\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0}|x| = 0\), by the Squeeze Theorem: \(\lim_{x \to 0} x\cos(1/x) = 0\)

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^4 \sin\left(\frac{3}{x}\right)\).

hints.text: Use \(-1 \le \sin(3/x) \le 1\) and multiply by \(x^4 \ge 0\).

solution_steps.text: Both bounds approach 0, so by the Squeeze Theorem the limit is 0.

problems.question_html: The Squeeze Theorem requires that the upper and lower bounding functions have the same limit. True or false?

hints.text: Review the statement of the Squeeze Theorem — what condition must \(g\) and \(h\) satisfy?

solution_steps.text: True. The Squeeze Theorem requires \(\lim g(x) = \lim h(x) = L\). Only then can we conclude \(\lim f(x) = L\).

problems.question_html: If \(3x - 1 \leq f(x) \leq x^2 + 2x - 1\) for all \(x\) near \(x = 1\), what is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\)?

hints.text: Evaluate the limits of the bounding functions at \(x = 1\). If they agree, the Squeeze Theorem gives the limit of \(f(x)\).
Lower bound: \(3(1) - 1 = 2\). Upper bound: \(1 + 2 - 1 = 2\). Both equal 2, so \(\lim f(x) = 2\).

solution_steps.text: Since both bounds approach 2 and \(3x - 1 \leq f(x) \leq x^2 + 2x - 1\), the Squeeze Theorem gives \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\).

problems.question_html: What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \cos\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\)?

hints.text: \(\cos\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\) oscillates, but \(x^2\) goes to 0. Use the Squeeze Theorem with bounds on cosine.
Since \(-1 \leq \cos\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \leq 1\), we get \(-x^2 \leq x^2\cos\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \leq x^2\). Both bounds go to 0.

solution_steps.text: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} (-x^2) = 0\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 = 0\). By the Squeeze Theorem, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \cos\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = 0\).

problems.question_html: Use the Squeeze Theorem to evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^4 \sin\!\left(\frac{3}{x^2}\right)\). State the bounding inequality, verify the bounds have the same limit, and conclude.
problems.sample_answer: Since -1 ≤ sin(3/x^2) ≤ 1 for all x ≠ 0, multiplying by x^4 ≥ 0 gives -x^4 ≤ x^4 sin(3/x^2) ≤ x^4. Both -x^4 and x^4 approach 0 as x→0, so by the Squeeze Theorem the limit is 0.
rubric: States the bounding inequality -x^4 ≤ x^4 sin(3/x^2) ≤ x^4
Verifies both bounding functions approach 0 as x→0
Correctly concludes the limit is 0 by the Squeeze Theorem

hints.text: Start with the universal bound \(-1 \leq \sin(\text{anything}) \leq 1\). Then multiply all parts by \(x^4\).
You get \(-x^4 \leq x^4 \sin\!\left(\frac{3}{x^2}\right) \leq x^4\). Both outer functions go to 0.

problems.correct_answer: Since -1 ≤ sin(3/x^2) ≤ 1 for all x ≠ 0, multiplying by x^4 ≥ 0 gives -x^4 ≤ x^4 sin(3/x^2) ≤ x^4. Both -x^4 and x^4 approach 0 as x→0, so by the Squeeze Theorem the limit is 0.

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = x \sin\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\) for \(x \neq 0\).

(a) Show that \(-|x| \leq f(x) \leq |x|\) for all \(x \neq 0\).

(b) Use the Squeeze Theorem to find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\).

(c) If we define \(f(0) = 0\), is \(f\) continuous at \(x = 0\)? Explain.
problems.sample_answer: (a) |sin(1/x)| ≤ 1, so |x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x|, giving -|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|. (b) Both bounds →0, so the limit is 0. (c) Yes, f(0)=0 = lim f(x), so f is continuous at 0.
rubric: Correctly establishes the inequality -|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|
Applies Squeeze Theorem to conclude the limit is 0
Verifies continuity: f(0) = 0 = lim f(x)

hints.text: Since \(|\sin(\theta)| \leq 1\) for any \(\theta\), we have \(|x \sin(1/x)| = |x| \cdot |\sin(1/x)| \leq |x|\).
This means \(-|x| \leq x \sin(1/x) \leq |x|\). Both \(-|x|\) and \(|x|\) go to 0 as \(x \to 0\).

solution_steps.text: (a) For all \(x \neq 0\): \(|\sin(1/x)| \leq 1\), so \(|x \sin(1/x)| = |x| \cdot |\sin(1/x)| \leq |x|\). This gives \(-|x| \leq x \sin(1/x) \leq |x|\).
(b) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} (-|x|) = 0\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} |x| = 0\). By the Squeeze Theorem, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x \sin(1/x) = 0\).
(c) With \(f(0) = 0\): (1) \(f(0) = 0\) ✓, (2) \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0\) ✓, (3) \(f(0) = \lim_{x \to 0} f(x)\) ✓. All three conditions for continuity are met, so \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).

problems.correct_answer: (a) |sin(1/x)| ≤ 1, so |x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x|, giving -|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|. (b) Both bounds →0, so the limit is 0. (c) Yes, f(0)=0 = lim f(x), so f is continuous at 0.

concepts.title: Connecting Multiple Representations of Limits
concepts.content_html:
Three Ways to Think About Limits

The AP exam tests your ability to work with limits across multiple representations:

  1. Analytical (algebraic): Evaluate limits using algebra, limit laws, and known results
  2. Graphical: Read or estimate limits from the graph of a function
  3. Numerical (tabular): Estimate limits from tables of values

Connecting Representations

A complete understanding of limits means you can:

  • Start with a graph and write the corresponding limit notation
  • Start with an algebraic expression and predict what the graph looks like near the limit point
  • Use a table to support or contradict an algebraic result
  • Recognize when different representations give the same (or different) information

Example: Three Views of One Limit

Consider \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}\) at \(x = 1\):

Algebraically: \(\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = x+1\) for \(x \neq 1\), so \(\lim_{x \to 1} = 2\).

Graphically: The graph is the line \(y = x + 1\) with a hole at \((1, 2)\). The curve approaches \(y = 2\) from both sides.

Numerically: A table of values shows \(f(0.9) = 1.9\), \(f(0.99) = 1.99\), \(f(1.01) = 2.01\), \(f(1.1) = 2.1\) — all approaching 2.

AP Exam Tip: Free-response questions often require you to justify your answer using a specific representation. "Justify using the graph" means reference visual features (approaching from left/right). "Justify analytically" means show the algebra. Know which representation the question is asking for.

problems.question_html: Analytically, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2-4}{x-2} = 4\). Which graphical feature corresponds to this?

choices.text: The graph has a hole at \((2, 4)\)
The graph has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 2\)

hints.text: The original function is undefined at \(x = 2\) (denominator is 0), but the limit exists.
An undefined point where the limit exists corresponds to a removable discontinuity — a hole in the graph.

solution_steps.text: \(f(x) = \frac{x^2-4}{x-2} = x+2\) for \(x \neq 2\). The graph is the line \(y = x+2\) with a hole at \(x = 2\).
The hole is at the point \((2, 4)\), which corresponds to the limit value.

problems.question_html: A table shows \(f(1.9) = 5.1\), \(f(1.99) = 5.01\), \(f(2.01) = 4.99\), \(f(2.1) = 4.9\). Which algebraic expression could produce these values near \(x = 2\)?

hints.text: The values approach 5 as \(x \to 2\), decreasing from left to right. What linear function passes through these points?

solution_steps.text: The table values suggest a limit of 5 and a decreasing linear trend near \(x=2\).

problems.question_html: If \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = 3\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = 3\), but \(f(a) = 5\), describe the graph at \(x = a\).

hints.text: The limit exists and equals 3, but the function value is 5. The limit and function value disagree.
This means there's an open circle at \((a, 3)\) and a solid dot at \((a, 5)\) — a removable discontinuity.

solution_steps.text: The graph has a hole (open circle) at \((a, 3)\) and a solid dot at \((a, 5)\).
This is a removable discontinuity — the limit exists but doesn't equal the function value.

problems.question_html: Which representation — graphical, numerical, or analytical — provides a rigorous proof that a limit equals a specific value?

hints.text: Graphs and tables rely on estimation and can miss subtle behavior.

solution_steps.text: Analytical (algebraic) methods provide rigorous proofs. Graphs and tables can only estimate — they sample finitely many points and can miss oscillation or other subtle behavior.

problems.question_html: A function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}\) for \(x \neq 1\). A table shows \(f(0.9) = 1.9\), \(f(0.99) = 1.99\), \(f(1.01) = 2.01\), \(f(1.1) = 2.1\). A graph shows a line with a hole at \((1, 2)\). What does the algebraic simplification \(\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = x + 1\) confirm?

choices.text: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\), consistent with the table and graph

hints.text: The algebraic simplification, table, and graph should all point to the same conclusion about the limit.
Algebraically, \(f(x) = x + 1\) for \(x \neq 1\), so \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\). This matches the table (values approaching 2) and the graph (hole at \((1,2)\)).

solution_steps.text: This is consistent with the table (values converge to 2) and the graph (hole at \((1,2)\) means the function approaches 2 but is not defined there).
Note: \(f(1)\) is undefined, so \(f\) is not continuous at 1. The limit exists even though the function value does not.

problems.question_html: A student claims \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 6\) based on a table. The graph of \(f\) shows a filled dot at \((2, 6)\) but a jump from \(y = 4\) on the left to \(y = 6\) on the right. Is the student's claim correct?

choices.text: Yes, because the right-hand limit is 6
No, because the left-hand limit is 4, not 6
No, because the function is not defined at \(x = 2\)

hints.text: The student may have only checked values from one side. Both one-sided limits must agree for the two-sided limit to exist.
The graph shows the left-hand limit is 4 and the right-hand limit is 6. Since \(4 \neq 6\), the two-sided limit does not exist.

solution_steps.text: The graph shows \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 4\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 6\).
Since \(4 \neq 6\), the two-sided limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\) does not exist.
The student likely only used values approaching 2 from the right in the table, missing the discrepancy. This shows why checking both sides is essential.

problems.question_html:
For the function \(f(x) = \frac{|x - 3|}{x - 3}\):

(a) Build a table of values using \(x = 2.9, 2.99, 3.01, 3.1\).

(b) Use algebra to find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x)\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x)\).

(c) Does \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) exist? Explain using all three representations (table, algebra, graph).
problems.sample_answer: (a) f(2.9)=-1, f(2.99)=-1, f(3.01)=1, f(3.1)=1. (b) For x<3: |x-3|=-(x-3), so f(x)=-1. For x>3: |x-3|=x-3, so f(x)=1. (c) Left limit=-1, right limit=1. The limit DNE. All three representations confirm this.
rubric: Correct table values: -1 for x < 3 and 1 for x > 3
Correctly analyzes the absolute value to get f(x)=-1 for x<3 and f(x)=1 for x>3
Concludes the limit DNE with consistent reasoning across all representations

solution_steps.text: (b) For \(x < 3\): \(|x-3| = -(x-3)\), so \(f(x) = -1\). Thus \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = -1\). For \(x > 3\): \(|x-3| = x-3\), so \(f(x) = 1\). Thus \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = 1\).

(c) Since \(-1 \neq 1\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) does not exist. The table shows a jump from \(-1\) to \(1\). The algebra confirms the piecewise constant behavior. The graph would show a horizontal line at \(y = -1\) for \(x < 3\) and \(y = 1\) for \(x > 3\) with a gap at \(x = 3\).

problems.correct_answer: (a) f(2.9)=-1, f(2.99)=-1, f(3.01)=1, f(3.1)=1. (b) For x<3: |x-3|=-(x-3), so f(x)=-1. For x>3: |x-3|=x-3, so f(x)=1. (c) Left limit=-1, right limit=1. The limit DNE. All three representations confirm this.

problems.question_html:
Consider \(g(x) = \frac{x^3 - 8}{x - 2}\).

(a) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} g(x)\) algebraically.

(b) Create a table with values \(x = 1.9, 1.99, 1.999, 2.001, 2.01, 2.1\) to verify.

(c) Describe what the graph of \(g\) looks like near \(x = 2\).
rubric: Correctly factors x^3 - 8 and evaluates the limit as 12
Provides table values that converge to 12 from both sides
Describes the graph as the parabola y = x^2 + 2x + 4 with a hole at (2, 12)

hints.text: Use the sum of cubes factoring: \(x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)\). Actually this is difference of cubes.
After canceling \((x - 2)\), evaluate \(x^2 + 2x + 4\) at \(x = 2\) to get \(4 + 4 + 4 = 12\).

solution_steps.text: (c) The graph of \(g\) looks like the parabola \(y = x^2 + 2x + 4\) with a hole at the point \((2, 12)\), since \(g\) is undefined at \(x = 2\).

concepts.title: Exploring Types of Discontinuities
concepts.content_html:
Types of Discontinuities

When a function fails to be continuous at a point \(x = a\), the type of discontinuity depends on how the continuity conditions fail.

Three Types

  1. Removable discontinuity (hole): The limit \(\lim_{x o a} f(x)\) exists, but either \(f(a)\) is undefined or \(f(a) eq \lim_{x o a} f(x)\).
    • Example: \(f(x) = rac{x^2-1}{x-1}\) at \(x = 1\). The limit is 2 but \(f(1)\) is undefined.
    • Called "removable" because you could redefine \(f(1) = 2\) to make it continuous.
  2. Jump discontinuity: Both one-sided limits exist but are not equal: \(\lim_{x o a^-} f(x) eq \lim_{x o a^+} f(x)\).
    • Common in piecewise functions.
    • Cannot be "fixed" by redefining \(f(a)\) — the jump is intrinsic to the function's behavior.
  3. Infinite discontinuity: At least one of the one-sided limits is \(\pm\infty\). This typically occurs at vertical asymptotes.
    • Example: \(f(x) = rac{1}{x}\) at \(x = 0\).
Classification Summary:
• Limit exists but \( eq f(a)\) â†' Removable
• One-sided limits exist but differ â†' Jump
• At least one side â†' \(\pm\infty\) â†' Infinite

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}\) has what type of discontinuity at \(x = 2\)?

hints.text: Factor and check if the limit exists at \(x = 2\).
\(\lim_{x \to 2}\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = 4\). The limit exists but \(f(2)\) is undefined.

solution_steps.text: Since the limit exists but the function is not defined there, this is a removable discontinuity.

problems.question_html: The function \(g(x) = \frac{1}{(x-3)^2}\) has what type of discontinuity at \(x = 3\)?

hints.text: What happens to \(\frac{1}{(x-3)^2}\) as \(x \to 3\)?

solution_steps.text: This is an infinite discontinuity (vertical asymptote at \(x = 3\)).

problems.question_html: A piecewise function is defined as \(f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1 & x < 1 \\ 5 & x \ge 1 \end{cases}\). Classify the discontinuity (if any) at \(x = 1\).

hints.text: Find the left-hand and right-hand limits at \(x = 1\).

solution_steps.text: Since \(3 \neq 5\), this is a jump discontinuity.

problems.question_html: Which type of discontinuity can be "fixed" by redefining the function value at the point?

hints.text: Think about which type has a limit that exists — you just need to set \(f(a)\) equal to that limit.
If the limit exists and equals \(L\), defining \(f(a) = L\) makes the function continuous. This is possible only for removable discontinuities.

solution_steps.text: A removable discontinuity can be fixed by defining (or redefining) \(f(a) = \lim_{x \to a} f(x)\).
Jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be fixed this way.

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 1 & \text{if } x < 2 \\ 5 & \text{if } x \geq 2 \end{cases}\) has a discontinuity at \(x = 2\). What type is it?

hints.text: Find both one-sided limits at \(x = 2\). If they differ, it's a jump discontinuity.
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 2 + 1 = 3\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 5\). Since \(3 \neq 5\), this is a jump discontinuity.

solution_steps.text: Since the one-sided limits exist but are not equal (\(3 \neq 5\)), this is a jump discontinuity.

problems.question_html: Which type of discontinuity does \(g(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}\) have at \(x = 2\)?

hints.text: Factor the numerator and check if the limit exists at \(x = 2\).
\(g(x) = \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x + 2\) for \(x \neq 2\). The limit is 4, but \(g(2)\) is undefined. This is removable.

solution_steps.text: The limit exists but the function is not defined at the point. This is a removable discontinuity  --  we could define \(g(2) = 4\) to make it continuous.

problems.question_html:
Classify and explain the discontinuity of each function at the given point.

(a) \(f(x) = \frac{1}{(x - 1)^2}\) at \(x = 1\)

(b) \(g(x) = \frac{x^2 - 9}{x + 3}\) at \(x = -3\)

(c) \(h(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & \text{if } x \leq 1 \\ 5 - x & \text{if } x > 1 \end{cases}\) at \(x = 1\)
problems.sample_answer: (a) Infinite: as x→1, 1/(x-1)^2→+∞. (b) Removable: limit = -6, but g(-3) undefined. (c) Jump: left limit = 2, right limit = 4, they differ.
rubric: Correctly classifies (a) as infinite with both sides going to +∞
Correctly classifies (b) as removable with limit = -6
Correctly classifies (c) as jump with left limit 2 ≠ right limit 4

hints.text: For each: check if the function is defined, find the limit(s), and compare. The three types are removable (limit exists, not equal to f(a)), jump (one-sided limits differ), and infinite (limit is ±∞).

solution_steps.text: (a) As \(x \to 1\), \((x-1)^2 \to 0^+\), so \(\frac{1}{(x-1)^2} \to +\infty\). This is an infinite discontinuity (vertical asymptote at \(x = 1\)).
(b) \(g(x) = \frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x+3} = x - 3\) for \(x \neq -3\). \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -3} g(x) = -3 - 3 = -6\), but \(g(-3)\) is undefined. This is a removable discontinuity.
(c) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^-} h(x) = 2(1) = 2\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^+} h(x) = 5 - 1 = 4\). Since \(2 \neq 4\), this is a jump discontinuity.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Infinite: as x→1, 1/(x-1)^2→+∞. (b) Removable: limit = -6, but g(-3) undefined. (c) Jump: left limit = 2, right limit = 4, they differ.

problems.question_html:
Give an example of a function with:

(a) a removable discontinuity at \(x = 0\)

(b) a jump discontinuity at \(x = 0\)

(c) an infinite discontinuity at \(x = 0\)

For each, state the function, verify it has the claimed discontinuity type, and explain why.
problems.sample_answer: (a) f(x) = x/x for x≠0  --  limit is 1 but f(0) undefined. (b) g(x) = x/|x| for x≠0  --  left limit = -1, right limit = 1. (c) h(x) = 1/x  --  approaches ±∞ from different sides.
rubric: Provides a valid function with a removable discontinuity at x = 0 with correct justification
Provides a valid function with a jump discontinuity at x = 0 with correct justification
Provides a valid function with an infinite discontinuity at x = 0 with correct justification

hints.text: For removable: the limit exists but the function is undefined or has a different value. For jump: one-sided limits exist but differ. For infinite: the function goes to ±∞.

Simple examples: (a) \(f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}\)  --  limit is 1 but undefined at 0. (b) \(g(x) = \frac{x}{|x|}\)  --  left limit \(-1\), right limit \(1\). (c) \(h(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}\)  --  goes to \(+\infty\).

solution_steps.text: (a) Removable: \(f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}\). \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\), but \(f(0)\) is undefined. Defining \(f(0) = 1\) removes the discontinuity.
(b) Jump: \(g(x) = \frac{x}{|x|}\). For \(x > 0\), \(g(x) = 1\). For \(x < 0\), \(g(x) = -1\). The one-sided limits are \(-1\) and \(1\), which differ.
(c) Infinite: \(h(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}\). As \(x \to 0\), \(\frac{1}{x^2} \to +\infty\). The function has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\).

problems.correct_answer: (a) f(x) = x/x for x≠0  --  limit is 1 but f(0) undefined. (b) g(x) = x/|x| for x≠0  --  left limit = -1, right limit = 1. (c) h(x) = 1/x  --  approaches ±∞ from different sides.

concepts.title: Defining Continuity at a Point
concepts.content_html:
The Definition of Continuity

Continuity is one of the most important concepts in calculus. Informally, a function is continuous if you can draw its graph without lifting your pencil. Formally:

Definition: A function \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\) if all three conditions are met:
1. \(f(a)\) is defined
2. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) exists
3. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)\)

If any one of these conditions fails, \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = a\).

Continuity of Common Functions

These functions are continuous on their entire domains:

  • Polynomials: continuous everywhere (all real numbers)
  • Rational functions \(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\): continuous wherever \(q(x) \neq 0\)
  • Trig functions: \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are continuous everywhere; \(\tan x\) is continuous except at odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)
  • Exponential and logarithmic: \(e^x\) is continuous everywhere; \(\ln x\) is continuous for \(x > 0\)
  • Root functions: \(\sqrt{x}\) is continuous for \(x \ge 0\); \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) is continuous everywhere

Continuity of Composed Functions

If \(f\) is continuous at \(b\) and \(\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = b\), then:

\[\lim_{x \to a} f(g(x)) = f\left(\lim_{x \to a} g(x)\right) = f(b)\]

In other words, you can "pass the limit inside" a continuous function.

problems.question_html: Which of the three conditions for continuity fails for \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) at \(x = 0\)?

choices.text: Condition 2: the limit does not exist
Condition 3: the limit does not equal \(f(0)\)

hints.text: What is \(f(0) = \frac{1}{0}\)?
Division by zero means \(f(0)\) is undefined — condition 1 fails immediately. (The limit also doesn't exist, but condition 1 failing is sufficient.)

solution_steps.text: Note: conditions 2 and 3 also fail (the limit is \(\pm\infty\)), but condition 1 is the first to fail.

problems.question_html: Is \(f(x) = |x|\) continuous at \(x = 0\)?

hints.text: Check all three conditions: (1) \(f(0) = 0\) âœ", (2) \(\lim_{x \to 0}|x| = ?\), (3) are they equal?
Both one-sided limits equal 0: \(|x| \to 0\) from both sides. All three conditions hold.

solution_steps.text: (3) \(\lim = 0 = f(0)\) âœ". All conditions met — \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).
Note: \(|x|\) has a corner at \(x = 0\) (not differentiable), but corners don't affect continuity.

problems.question_html: Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x \neq 3 \\ 10 & x = 3 \end{cases}\). Is \(f\) continuous at \(x = 3\)?

hints.text: Check condition 3: does the limit equal \(f(3)\)?
\(\lim_{x \to 3} x^2 = 9\), but \(f(3) = 10\). Since \(9 \neq 10\), condition 3 fails.

solution_steps.text: Not continuous — this is a removable discontinuity.

problems.question_html: For what value of \(k\) is \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 1 & x < 2 \\ kx - 1 & x \ge 2 \end{cases}\) continuous at \(x = 2\)?

hints.text: For continuity, the left-hand limit must equal the right-hand limit (and equal \(f(2)\)).
Left: \(2 + 1 = 3\). Right: \(2k - 1\). Set \(2k - 1 = 3\) and solve.

problems.question_html: Which of the following functions is continuous at \(x = 2\)?

hints.text: Check all three conditions: (1) \(f(a)\) is defined, (2) \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) exists, (3) they are equal.
For \(g\): \(\lim_{x \to 2} (x+1) = 3 = g(2)\). All three conditions are met. The others fail at least one condition.

solution_steps.text: \(f(x) = \frac{x^2-4}{x-2}\): undefined at \(x = 2\). Fails condition 1. Not continuous.

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = \begin{cases} ax + 1 & \text{if } x \leq 3 \\ x^2 - 2 & \text{if } x > 3 \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 3\). What is the value of \(a\)?

hints.text: For continuity, the left-hand limit must equal the right-hand limit and equal \(f(3)\).
From the right: \(3^2 - 2 = 7\). From the left (and \(f(3)\)): \(3a + 1\). Set \(3a + 1 = 7\), so \(a = 2\).

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^2 - 4x + 3}{x - 3} & \text{if } x \neq 3 \\ k & \text{if } x = 3 \end{cases}\).

(a) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\).

(b) Find the value of \(k\) that makes \(f\) continuous at \(x = 3\).

(c) Verify all three conditions for continuity with your chosen \(k\).
problems.sample_answer: (a) Factor: (x-3)(x-1)/(x-3) = x-1. Limit = 2. (b) k = 2. (c) f(3) = 2, lim f(x) = 2, and 2 = 2. All three conditions met.
rubric: Correctly factors and finds the limit as 2
Sets k = 2 for continuity
Verifies all three conditions for continuity explicitly

hints.text: Factor the numerator \(x^2 - 4x + 3\) and cancel the common factor with the denominator.
\(x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x-3)(x-1)\). So \(f(x) = x - 1\) for \(x \neq 3\), and the limit is \(2\).

solution_steps.text: (b) For continuity at \(x = 3\), we need \(f(3) = \lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\), so \(k = 2\).
(c) With \(k = 2\): (1) \(f(3) = 2\) is defined ✓. (2) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 2\) exists ✓. (3) \(f(3) = 2 = \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) ✓. All three conditions hold.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Factor: (x-3)(x-1)/(x-3) = x-1. Limit = 2. (b) k = 2. (c) f(3) = 2, lim f(x) = 2, and 2 = 2. All three conditions met.

problems.question_html:
Let \(g(x) = \begin{cases} cx^2 + 1 & \text{if } x < -1 \\ 3cx - 2 & \text{if } x \geq -1 \end{cases}\).

(a) Find all values of \(c\) that make \(g\) continuous at \(x = -1\).

(b) For each value of \(c\) found, verify continuity by checking all three conditions.
problems.sample_answer: Left limit: c(-1)^2 + 1 = c + 1. Right limit and g(-1): 3c(-1) - 2 = -3c - 2. Set equal: c + 1 = -3c - 2, so 4c = -3, c = -3/4.
rubric: Correctly computes left-hand limit as c + 1
Correctly computes right-hand limit as -3c - 2
Solves c + 1 = -3c - 2 to get c = -3/4 and verifies all conditions

hints.text: Set the left-hand limit equal to the right-hand limit (which equals \(g(-1)\) since the second piece uses \(\geq\)).

problems.correct_answer: Left limit: c(-1)^2 + 1 = c + 1. Right limit and g(-1): 3c(-1) - 2 = -3c - 2. Set equal: c + 1 = -3c - 2, so 4c = -3, c = -3/4.

concepts.title: Confirming Continuity over an Interval
concepts.content_html:
Continuity on an Interval

We say \(f\) is continuous on an open interval \((a, b)\) if it is continuous at every point in that interval.

For a closed interval \([a, b]\), we also need:

  • \(f\) is continuous on \((a, b)\)
  • \(f\) is right-continuous at \(a\): \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)\)
  • \(f\) is left-continuous at \(b\): \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)\)

Continuous Everywhere

A function is continuous everywhere (or just "continuous") if it is continuous at every point in its domain. Examples:

  • All polynomials
  • \(\sin x\), \(\cos x\), \(e^x\)

How to Confirm Continuity

To show \(f\) is continuous on an interval:

  1. Identify the type of function on each piece (polynomial, rational, trig, etc.)
  2. Check that each piece is continuous on its sub-interval
  3. At any "break points" (where the formula changes), verify the three continuity conditions
Key Fact: If \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(x = a\), then \(f + g\), \(f - g\), \(f \cdot g\), and \(\frac{f}{g}\) (when \(g(a) \neq 0\)) are all continuous at \(x = a\). Also, \(f \circ g\) (composition) is continuous if both are continuous.

problems.question_html: On which interval is \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x-3}\) continuous?

hints.text: Where is \(f(x)\) undefined?
\(f\) is undefined at \(x = 3\). It's continuous on any interval not containing 3.

solution_steps.text: \(f\) is a rational function, continuous everywhere except where the denominator is 0, i.e., at \(x = 3\).
\((0, 3)\) does not contain \(x = 3\), so \(f\) is continuous on \((0, 3)\). The interval \([0, 5]\) contains 3, so \(f\) is not continuous there.

problems.question_html: Is \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) continuous on \([0, \infty)\)?

choices.text: No, because \(f\) is not defined for \(x < 0\)

hints.text: The domain of \(\sqrt{x}\) is \([0, \infty)\). Is it continuous at every point in this domain?
At \(x = 0\): right-continuous (\(\lim_{x \to 0^+} \sqrt{x} = 0 = f(0)\)). For \(x > 0\): continuous (root function).

solution_steps.text: \(\sqrt{x}\) is continuous on \((0, \infty)\) as a root function.

problems.question_html: Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + 1 & x \le 1 \\ 3x - 1 & x > 1 \end{cases}\). Is \(f\) continuous on \([0, 3]\)?

hints.text: Both pieces are polynomials (continuous). Check the break point at \(x = 1\).
Left: \(1^2+1=2\). Right: \(3(1)-1=2\). Since they match and \(f(1)=2\), it's continuous.

solution_steps.text: Both pieces are polynomials, so each is continuous on its interval.
All three continuity conditions hold at \(x = 1\), so \(f\) is continuous on \([0, 3]\).

problems.question_html: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and \(g\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), is \(f + g\) continuous on \([a, b]\)?

choices.text: Only if \(f\) and \(g\) are both polynomials

hints.text: The sum of continuous functions is continuous — this is one of the basic continuity theorems.

solution_steps.text: By the sum rule for continuity, if \(f\) and \(g\) are both continuous at a point, then \(f + g\) is also continuous at that point.
Since this holds for every point in \([a, b]\), \(f + g\) is continuous on \([a, b]\).

problems.question_html: On which interval is \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 3}\) continuous?

hints.text: The function is undefined at \(x = 3\). Where is it continuous?
\(f\) is continuous on \((-\infty, 3)\) and \((3, \infty)\). Of the choices, \((3, \infty)\) is entirely in the domain.

solution_steps.text: \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x-3}\) is undefined at \(x = 3\). The domain is \((-\infty, 3) \cup (3, \infty)\).
As a rational function, \(f\) is continuous everywhere it is defined, so it is continuous on \((-\infty, 3)\) and \((3, \infty)\).
Among the choices, \((3, \infty)\) is the only interval entirely within the domain. \([0, 5]\) contains \(x = 3\), and \([3, \infty)\) includes the endpoint \(x = 3\) where \(f\) is undefined.

problems.question_html: The function \(g(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^2}\) is defined on \([-2, 2]\). Is \(g\) continuous on this closed interval?
