choices.text: No, because \(g\) involves a square root
No, because \(g\) is not differentiable at the endpoints
Yes, because \(g\) is continuous on \((-2, 2)\) and has correct one-sided limits at the endpoints
Yes, but only on the open interval \((-2, 2)\)

hints.text: Continuity on \([a, b]\) requires continuity on \((a, b)\), right-continuity at \(a\), and left-continuity at \(b\).

solution_steps.text: The domain of \(g(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^2}\) is \([-2, 2]\) since we need \(4 - x^2 \geq 0\).
On \((-2, 2)\), \(g\) is a composition of continuous functions (polynomial under a square root with positive radicand), so it's continuous.
At \(x = -2\): \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -2^+} \sqrt{4 - x^2} = \sqrt{0} = 0 = g(-2)\). At \(x = 2\): \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^-} \sqrt{4 - x^2} = 0 = g(2)\).
All conditions for continuity on \([-2, 2]\) are satisfied.

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & \text{if } 0 \leq x \leq 2 \\ 6 - x & \text{if } 2 < x \leq 5 \end{cases}\).

(a) Is \(f\) continuous on \([0, 2]\)? On \((2, 5]\)?

(b) Is \(f\) continuous on \([0, 5]\)? If not, identify the discontinuity and its type.
problems.sample_answer: (a) Yes on [0,2] (polynomial, continuous). Yes on (2,5] (linear, continuous). (b) Not continuous on [0,5] because at x=2: left limit = 4, right limit = 4, f(2) = 4. Wait  --  actually it IS continuous at x=2. Check: lim(x→2⁻) = 4, lim(x→2⁺) = 6-2=4, f(2)=4. So f is continuous on [0,5].
rubric: Correctly verifies continuity on [0,2] and (2,5] separately
Checks continuity at x = 2 by computing both one-sided limits and f(2)
Correctly concludes f is continuous on [0,5] since all values agree at x = 2

hints.text: Each piece is continuous on its interval. The only question is what happens at the boundary \(x = 2\).
At \(x = 2\): left limit \(= 2^2 = 4\), right limit \(= 6 - 2 = 4\), \(f(2) = 4\). All equal!

solution_steps.text: (a) \(f(x) = x^2\) on \([0, 2]\) is a polynomial, hence continuous. \(f(x) = 6 - x\) on \((2, 5]\) is linear, hence continuous.
(b) At the boundary \(x = 2\): \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^-} x^2 = 4\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^+} (6 - x) = 4\), and \(f(2) = 2^2 = 4\).
Since left limit = right limit = \(f(2) = 4\), \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\). Therefore \(f\) is continuous on the entire interval \([0, 5]\).

problems.correct_answer: (a) Yes on [0,2] (polynomial, continuous). Yes on (2,5] (linear, continuous). (b) Not continuous on [0,5] because at x=2: left limit = 4, right limit = 4, f(2) = 4. Wait  --  actually it IS continuous at x=2. Check: lim(x→2⁻) = 4, lim(x→2⁺) = 6-2=4, f(2)=4. So f is continuous on [0,5].

problems.question_html: Determine whether \(f(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x + 1}}\) is continuous on the interval \([-1, \infty)\). State which theorems or properties of continuous functions you use.
problems.sample_answer: The domain requires x + 1 > 0 (for the denominator), so x > -1, but at x = -1 the denominator is 0 and the function is undefined. So f is continuous on (-1, ∞) but NOT on [-1, ∞) since f(-1) is undefined.
rubric: Identifies that f(-1) is undefined because the denominator is 0
Concludes f is continuous on (-1, ∞) but not on [-1, ∞)
Uses properties of quotients and compositions of continuous functions

hints.text: Check whether \(f(-1)\) is defined. The denominator is \(\sqrt{x + 1}\)  --  what happens at \(x = -1\)?
At \(x = -1\): \(\sqrt{-1 + 1} = \sqrt{0} = 0\). Division by zero, so \(f(-1)\) is undefined. \(f\) cannot be continuous at \(x = -1\).

solution_steps.text: At \(x = -1\): \(\sqrt{-1 + 1} = 0\), so the denominator is 0 and \(f(-1)\) is undefined.
For \(x > -1\): the numerator \(x\) is continuous (polynomial), and \(\sqrt{x+1}\) is continuous and positive. Their quotient is continuous.
Therefore \(f\) is continuous on \((-1, \infty)\) but not on \([-1, \infty)\) because \(f\) is not defined at the left endpoint.

problems.correct_answer: The domain requires x + 1 > 0 (for the denominator), so x > -1, but at x = -1 the denominator is 0 and the function is undefined. So f is continuous on (-1, ∞) but NOT on [-1, ∞) since f(-1) is undefined.

concepts.title: Removing Discontinuities
concepts.content_html:
Removing Discontinuities

A removable discontinuity at \(x = a\) means the limit \(\lim_{x o a} f(x) = L\) exists, but \(f(a) eq L\) (or \(f(a)\) is undefined). We can "remove" the discontinuity by defining or redefining \(f(a) = L\).

Method

  1. Find \(\displaystyle L = \lim_{x o a} f(x)\) using algebraic techniques (factoring, conjugate, etc.)
  2. Define the extended function: \(F(x) = egin{cases} f(x) & x eq a \ L & x = a \end{cases}\)
  3. \(F\) is now continuous at \(x = a\)

Example

\(f(x) = rac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}\) is undefined at \(x = 3\).

\(\lim_{x o 3} f(x) = \lim_{x o 3}(x+3) = 6\)

Define \(F(x) = egin{cases} rac{x^2-9}{x-3} & x eq 3 \ 6 & x = 3 \end{cases}\)

Now \(F\) is continuous at \(x = 3\).

Finding the Value That Makes a Piecewise Function Continuous

A common AP problem: given a piecewise function with an unknown constant, find the value that makes it continuous.

Strategy: Set the left-hand limit equal to the right-hand limit (and equal to the function value at the break point).

AP Exam Tip: When finding \(k\) to make a piecewise function continuous, you need \(\lim_{x o a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x o a^+} f(x) = f(a)\). Write out each side, set them equal, and solve for \(k\).

problems.question_html: What value should be assigned to \(f(4)\) to make \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 16}{x - 4}\) continuous at \(x = 4\)?

hints.text: Find \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)\) by factoring.

solution_steps.text: Setting \(f(4) = 8\) makes the function continuous at \(x = 4\).

problems.question_html: Find the value of \(c\) so that \(f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + c & x < 3 \\ x^2 & x \ge 3 \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 3\).

hints.text: Set the left-hand limit equal to the function value at \(x = 3\).

problems.question_html: Find the value of \(a\) so that \(f(x) = \begin{cases} ax^2 & x \le 2 \\ 4x + 4 & x > 2 \end{cases}\) is continuous.

hints.text: At \(x = 2\): left side = \(a(4) = 4a\), right side = \(4(2) + 4 = 12\).

problems.question_html: Can a jump discontinuity be removed by redefining \(f(a)\)?

hints.text: What's the defining feature of a jump discontinuity?
The left-hand and right-hand limits differ. No single value of \(f(a)\) can equal both.

solution_steps.text: No. A jump discontinuity has \(\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)\).
Since the two-sided limit doesn't exist, redefining \(f(a)\) cannot make the function continuous.

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 + x - 6}{x - 2}\) has a removable discontinuity at \(x = 2\). What value should be assigned to \(f(2)\) to make \(f\) continuous?

hints.text: Factor the numerator and simplify. The limit at \(x = 2\) gives the value needed.

solution_steps.text: Defining \(f(2) = 5\) makes \(f\) continuous at \(x = 2\) since \(f(2) = \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\).

problems.question_html: Which type of discontinuity can be "removed" by redefining the function at a single point?

hints.text: A removable discontinuity occurs when the limit exists but doesn't equal the function value (or the function is undefined).
Only a removable discontinuity can be fixed by changing one point: set \(f(a)\) equal to the existing limit. Jump and infinite discontinuities require more fundamental changes.

solution_steps.text: A removable discontinuity is one where \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) exists, but \(f(a) \neq L\) or \(f(a)\) is undefined.

By redefining \(f(a) = L\), we satisfy all three conditions for continuity. Jump discontinuities have unequal one-sided limits, and infinite discontinuities have limits of \(\pm\infty\)  --  neither can be fixed by redefining a single value.

problems.question_html:
The function \(g(x) = \frac{x^3 - 27}{x^2 - 9}\) is undefined at \(x = 3\) and \(x = -3\).

(a) Can the discontinuity at \(x = 3\) be removed? If so, find the value to assign.

(b) Can the discontinuity at \(x = -3\) be removed? If so, find the value. If not, explain why.
problems.sample_answer: (a) Factor: (x-3)(x^2+3x+9)/[(x-3)(x+3)] = (x^2+3x+9)/(x+3). At x=3: 27/6 = 9/2. Removable; assign g(3)=9/2. (b) At x=-3: limit = (9-9+9)/(−3+3) = 9/0, which is infinite. Not removable.
rubric: Correctly factors and simplifies to find the limit at x = 3 is 9/2
States the discontinuity at x = 3 is removable with g(3) = 9/2
Shows the limit at x = -3 does not exist (infinite) and the discontinuity is not removable

solution_steps.text: (a) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2+3x+9}{x+3} = \frac{9+9+9}{6} = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}\). The discontinuity at \(x = 3\) is removable. Assign \(g(3) = \frac{9}{2}\).
(b) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -3} \frac{x^2+3x+9}{x+3} = \frac{9 - 9 + 9}{0} = \frac{9}{0}\), which diverges. The discontinuity at \(x = -3\) is infinite (vertical asymptote) and cannot be removed.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Factor: (x-3)(x^2+3x+9)/[(x-3)(x+3)] = (x^2+3x+9)/(x+3). At x=3: 27/6 = 9/2. Removable; assign g(3)=9/2. (b) At x=-3: limit = (9-9+9)/(−3+3) = 9/0, which is infinite. Not removable.

problems.question_html: Define a function \(F(x)\) that is continuous everywhere and agrees with \(f(x) = \frac{2x^2 + x - 3}{x - 1}\) wherever \(f\) is defined. Show all steps.
problems.sample_answer: Factor: 2x^2 + x - 3 = (2x+3)(x-1). So f(x) = 2x+3 for x ≠ 1. The limit at x=1 is 5. Define F(x) = 2x + 3 for all x. This is continuous everywhere and equals f(x) for x ≠ 1.
rubric: Correctly factors the numerator as (2x + 3)(x - 1)
Finds the limit at x = 1 is 5
Defines F(x) = 2x + 3 as a continuous extension

hints.text: Factor the numerator. The continuous extension is the simplified form evaluated everywhere.

solution_steps.text: Define \(F(x) = 2x + 3\) for all real \(x\). This is a polynomial and is continuous everywhere. For \(x \neq 1\), \(F(x) = f(x)\), and at \(x = 1\), \(F(1) = 5 = \lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\).

problems.correct_answer: Factor: 2x^2 + x - 3 = (2x+3)(x-1). So f(x) = 2x+3 for x ≠ 1. The limit at x=1 is 5. Define F(x) = 2x + 3 for all x. This is continuous everywhere and equals f(x) for x ≠ 1.

concepts.title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
concepts.content_html:
Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes

When a function grows without bound near a point, we describe this using infinite limits.

Definition:
• \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \infty\) means \(f(x)\) grows positively without bound as \(x \to a\)
• \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = -\infty\) means \(f(x)\) decreases without bound as \(x \to a\)

In either case, the vertical line \(x = a\) is a vertical asymptote of \(f\).

Determining the Sign

For a rational function near a vertical asymptote, analyze the sign of the numerator and denominator:

  1. Find where the denominator is zero (potential vertical asymptotes)
  2. Check that the numerator is nonzero there (if both are zero, it might be a hole instead)
  3. Test signs just to the left and right of the asymptote to determine if the function goes to \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\)

Example

\(f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 2\).

  • As \(x \to 2^+\): denominator is small and positive â†' \(f(x) \to +\infty\)
  • As \(x \to 2^-\): denominator is small and negative â†' \(f(x) \to -\infty\)

So \(\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = +\infty\) and \(\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = -\infty\). The two-sided limit DNE.

Even vs. Odd Multiplicity

If the denominator factor has even multiplicity (e.g., \((x-a)^2\)), the function goes to \(+\infty\) (or \(-\infty\)) from both sides. If odd multiplicity (e.g., \((x-a)^1\)), the signs differ on each side.
concepts.content_raw: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes

problem_sets.title: Practice: Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes

problems.question_html: What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1}{x}\)?

hints.text: As \(x\) approaches 0 from the right, \(x\) is small and positive.
\(\frac{1}{\text{small positive}} = \text{large positive} \to +\infty\).

problems.question_html: Find all vertical asymptotes of \(f(x) = \frac{x+1}{x^2 - 4}\).

hints.text: Set the denominator equal to zero: \(x^2 - 4 = 0\).
\(x = \pm 2\). Check that the numerator is nonzero at these points: \(f(2) = \frac{3}{0}\) and \(f(-2) = \frac{-1}{0}\). Both are vertical asymptotes.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1^-} \frac{x}{(x-1)^2}\).

hints.text: The denominator \((x-1)^2\) has even multiplicity. What does this mean for the sign?
\((x-1)^2 > 0\) regardless of the side. Numerator is near 1 (positive). So \(\frac{\text{positive}}{\text{small positive}} \to +\infty\).

solution_steps.text: As \(x \to 1^-\): numerator \(\to 1 > 0\), denominator \((x-1)^2 \to 0^+\) (always positive due to squaring)

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\) does NOT have a vertical asymptote at \(x = 1\). Why?

hints.text: Factor the numerator and see what happens.
\(x^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1)\). The \((x-1)\) cancels, leaving a hole, not an asymptote.

solution_steps.text: The common factor cancels, so there's a removable discontinuity (hole) at \(x = 1\), not a vertical asymptote.
\(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\), which is finite — no vertical asymptote.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{5}{x^2}\).

hints.text: As \(x \to 0^+\), \(x^2 \to 0^+\), so \(\frac{5}{x^2}\) becomes a positive number divided by a very small positive number.
\(\frac{5}{x^2} \to \frac{5}{0^+} = +\infty\). The function grows without bound.

solution_steps.text: Therefore \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{5}{x^2} = +\infty\). There is a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\).

problems.question_html: How many vertical asymptotes does \(f(x) = \frac{x + 1}{x^2 - 4}\) have?

hints.text: Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not zero.
\(x^2 - 4 = 0\) when \(x = \pm 2\). At \(x = 2\): numerator = 3 (nonzero). At \(x = -2\): numerator = \(-1\) (nonzero). Both are vertical asymptotes.

solution_steps.text: Factor: \(x^2 - 4 = (x-2)(x+2)\). Denominator is zero at \(x = 2\) and \(x = -2\).

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = \frac{x - 1}{(x - 1)(x + 2)}\).

(a) Find all points where \(f\) is undefined.

(b) Determine which are vertical asymptotes and which are removable discontinuities.

(c) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -2^-} f(x)\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -2^+} f(x)\).
problems.sample_answer: (a) Undefined at x=1 and x=-2. (b) At x=1: cancel (x-1), limit = 1/3, removable. At x=-2: 1/(x+2) has VA. (c) From left: 1/(0⁻) = −∞. From right: 1/(0⁺) = +∞.
rubric: Identifies both x = 1 and x = -2 as points where f is undefined
Correctly classifies x = 1 as removable and x = -2 as a vertical asymptote
Correctly evaluates both one-sided limits at x = -2

hints.text: Cancel any common factors first. What remains in the denominator determines vertical asymptotes.
\(f(x) = \frac{1}{x+2}\) for \(x \neq 1\). At \(x = 1\): removable (limit is \(\frac{1}{3}\)). At \(x = -2\): vertical asymptote.

solution_steps.text: (a) \(f\) is undefined where \((x-1)(x+2) = 0\), i.e., at \(x = 1\) and \(x = -2\).

(b) Cancel \((x-1)\): \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x+2}\) for \(x \neq 1\). At \(x = 1\): \(\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{1}{x+2} = \frac{1}{3}\). Removable discontinuity. At \(x = -2\): \(\frac{1}{x+2} \to \pm\infty\). Vertical asymptote.

problems.correct_answer: (a) Undefined at x=1 and x=-2. (b) At x=1: cancel (x-1), limit = 1/3, removable. At x=-2: 1/(x+2) has VA. (c) From left: 1/(0⁻) = −∞. From right: 1/(0⁺) = +∞.

problems.question_html:
Analyze the vertical asymptotes of \(g(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 - 2x + 1}\).

(a) Factor numerator and denominator.

(b) Simplify and identify all vertical asymptotes and removable discontinuities.

(c) Find the limit as \(x\) approaches each point of discontinuity from both sides.
problems.sample_answer: (a) Num: (x-1)(x+1). Denom: (x-1)^2. (b) g(x) = (x+1)/(x-1) for x≠1. x=1 is a VA (not removable since factor remains). (c) From left: 2/0⁻ = −∞. From right: 2/0⁺ = +∞.
rubric: Correctly factors both as (x-1)(x+1) and (x-1)^2
Simplifies to (x+1)/(x-1) and identifies x=1 as a vertical asymptote (not removable)
Correctly evaluates both one-sided limits at x = 1

hints.text: Factor carefully: \(x^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1)\) and \(x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x-1)^2\).
One factor of \((x-1)\) cancels, leaving \(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\). One factor remains, creating a vertical asymptote.

solution_steps.text: (b) \(g(x) = \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{x+1}{x-1}\) for \(x \neq 1\). One \((x-1)\) factor remains in the denominator, so \(x = 1\) is a vertical asymptote (not removable).

problems.correct_answer: (a) Num: (x-1)(x+1). Denom: (x-1)^2. (b) g(x) = (x+1)/(x-1) for x≠1. x=1 is a VA (not removable since factor remains). (c) From left: 2/0⁻ = −∞. From right: 2/0⁺ = +∞.

concepts.title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
concepts.content_html:
Limits at Infinity

While infinite limits describe behavior near a point, limits at infinity describe behavior as \(x\) grows without bound.

Definition:
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L\) means \(f(x)\) approaches \(L\) as \(x\) grows positively without bound.
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L\) means \(f(x)\) approaches \(L\) as \(x\) decreases without bound.

If either limit equals \(L\), the line \(y = L\) is a horizontal asymptote.

Rules for Rational Functions

For \(f(x) = \frac{a_n x^n + \ldots}{b_m x^m + \ldots}\):

  • Degree of numerator < degree of denominator (\(n < m\)): \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} f(x) = 0\). Horizontal asymptote: \(y = 0\).
  • Degree of numerator = degree of denominator (\(n = m\)): \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} f(x) = \frac{a_n}{b_m}\). Horizontal asymptote: \(y = \frac{a_n}{b_m}\).
  • Degree of numerator > degree of denominator (\(n > m\)): the limit is \(\pm\infty\). No horizontal asymptote.

Technique: Divide by Highest Power

To evaluate a limit at infinity for a rational function, divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of \(x\) in the denominator.

Example: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{5x^2 - 3}{2x^2 + x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{5 - 3/x^2}{2 + 1/x} = \frac{5}{2}\)

Non-Rational Functions

Some important limits at infinity:

  • \(\lim_{x \to \infty} e^x = \infty\) and \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} e^x = 0\) (horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) on the left)
  • \(\lim_{x \to \infty} \ln x = \infty\) (no horizontal asymptote)
concepts.content_raw: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^2 + 2x}{5x^2 - 1}\).

hints.text: Same degree (both degree 2). Compare leading coefficients.

problems.question_html: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + 1}{x^3 - 2}\).

hints.text: Degree of numerator (1) < degree of denominator (3).
When the bottom grows faster, the fraction goes to 0.

problems.question_html: What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} e^x\)?

hints.text: As \(x\) becomes very negative, \(e^x\) becomes \(e^{-\text{large}}\), which is very small.
\(e^x \to 0^+\) as \(x \to -\infty\).

solution_steps.text: \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} e^x = 0\). The exponential function decays to 0 as \(x \to -\infty\).
The line \(y = 0\) is a horizontal asymptote on the left.

problems.question_html: Find all horizontal asymptotes of \(f(x) = \frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}\).

hints.text: Check both \(x \to +\infty\) and \(x \to -\infty\). Be careful with \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\).
For \(x \to +\infty\): \(\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \approx \frac{2x}{x} = 2\). For \(x \to -\infty\): \(\frac{2x}{|x|} = \frac{2x}{-x} = -2\).

problems.question_html: What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{5x^3 + 2x}{3x^3 - x^2 + 1}\)?

hints.text: When the degrees of numerator and denominator are equal, the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients.
Both are degree 3. Leading coefficients: \(5\) and \(3\). Limit \(= \frac{5}{3}\).

solution_steps.text: Numerator degree: 3 (leading coefficient 5). Denominator degree: 3 (leading coefficient 3).
Since the degrees are equal, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{5x^3 + 2x}{3x^3 - x^2 + 1} = \frac{5}{3}\).

problems.question_html: What is the horizontal asymptote of \(f(x) = \frac{4x^2 + 1}{2x^3 - x}\)?

hints.text: Compare the degree of the numerator to the degree of the denominator.
Numerator degree 2 < denominator degree 3, so the limit at infinity is 0. The horizontal asymptote is \(y = 0\).

solution_steps.text: Since the numerator degree is less than the denominator degree, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} f(x) = 0\).

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = \frac{2x^2 - x + 3}{x + 1}\).

(a) Does \(f\) have a horizontal asymptote? Explain using the degrees.

(b) Perform polynomial long division to write \(f(x)\) in the form \(q(x) + \frac{r}{x + 1}\).

(c) Use your result to describe the end behavior of \(f\).
problems.sample_answer: (a) No HA because degree of numerator (2) > degree of denominator (1). (b) 2x^2 - x + 3 = (x+1)(2x - 3) + 6, so f(x) = 2x - 3 + 6/(x+1). (c) As x→±∞, 6/(x+1)→0, so f(x) ≈ 2x - 3. The line y = 2x - 3 is a slant asymptote.
rubric: Correctly states no horizontal asymptote because numerator degree > denominator degree
Correctly performs long division to get f(x) = 2x - 3 + 6/(x+1)
Identifies y = 2x - 3 as a slant (oblique) asymptote

hints.text: When the numerator degree exceeds the denominator degree by 1, the function has a slant asymptote instead of a horizontal one.
Divide: \(2x^2 - x + 3\) by \(x + 1\). First term: \(2x\). Remainder after subtracting \(2x(x+1) = 2x^2 + 2x\): \(-3x + 3\). Next term: \(-3\). Remainder: \(6\).

solution_steps.text: (a) Numerator degree 2 > denominator degree 1, so there is no horizontal asymptote (\(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty\)).
(c) As \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(\frac{6}{x+1} \to 0\), so \(f(x) \to 2x - 3\). The line \(y = 2x - 3\) is a slant (oblique) asymptote.

problems.correct_answer: (a) No HA because degree of numerator (2) > degree of denominator (1). (b) 2x^2 - x + 3 = (x+1)(2x - 3) + 6, so f(x) = 2x - 3 + 6/(x+1). (c) As x→±∞, 6/(x+1)→0, so f(x) ≈ 2x - 3. The line y = 2x - 3 is a slant asymptote.

problems.question_html: Find all horizontal asymptotes of \(g(x) = \frac{3x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}\) by evaluating \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} g(x)\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x)\).
problems.sample_answer: As x→∞: divide by x (positive): 3x/(x·sqrt(1+4/x^2)) = 3/sqrt(1+4/x^2) → 3. As x→−∞: divide by |x| = -x: 3x/(-x·sqrt(1+4/x^2)) = -3/sqrt(1+4/x^2) → -3. Two horizontal asymptotes: y=3 and y=-3.
rubric: Correctly evaluates the limit as x→+∞ to get 3
Correctly handles the sign when x→−∞ to get -3
States both horizontal asymptotes y = 3 and y = -3

hints.text: Divide numerator and denominator by \(|x|\). Remember \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\), which equals \(x\) when \(x > 0\) and \(-x\) when \(x < 0\).

solution_steps.text: There are two horizontal asymptotes: \(y = 3\) (as \(x \to +\infty\)) and \(y = -3\) (as \(x \to -\infty\)).

problems.correct_answer: As x→∞: divide by x (positive): 3x/(x·sqrt(1+4/x^2)) = 3/sqrt(1+4/x^2) → 3. As x→−∞: divide by |x| = -x: 3x/(-x·sqrt(1+4/x^2)) = -3/sqrt(1+4/x^2) → -3. Two horizontal asymptotes: y=3 and y=-3.

concepts.title: Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
concepts.content_html:
The Intermediate Value Theorem

The IVT is the first major existence theorem in calculus. It guarantees that a continuous function hits every value between its endpoint values.

Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT): If \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and \(N\) is any number between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\), then there exists at least one \(c \in (a, b)\) such that \(f(c) = N\).

What IVT Says (Intuitively)

If you walk continuously from one elevation to another, you must pass through every elevation in between. You can't teleport over any value.

Using IVT to Show a Root Exists

The most common application: proving that a function has a zero (root) in an interval.

Strategy:

  1. Show \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\)
  2. Show \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs (one positive, one negative)
  3. Conclude: by IVT, there exists \(c \in (a, b)\) with \(f(c) = 0\)

Example

Show that \(f(x) = x^3 - 4x + 1\) has a root in \([0, 1]\).

  • \(f\) is a polynomial â†' continuous everywhere âœ"
  • \(f(0) = 1 > 0\)
  • \(f(1) = 1 - 4 + 1 = -2 < 0\)

Since \(f(0) > 0 > f(1)\) and \(f\) is continuous, by IVT there exists \(c \in (0, 1)\) with \(f(c) = 0\).

Important Notes

  • IVT requires continuity — it fails for discontinuous functions
  • IVT guarantees existence ("there exists"), not uniqueness — there may be multiple values of \(c\)
  • IVT does NOT tell you what \(c\) is — only that it exists
AP Exam Tip: On free-response questions, when using IVT you must explicitly state: (1) \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), (2) \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) straddle the target value \(N\), (3) therefore by IVT, \(c\) exists. Skipping any part may cost you points.
concepts.content_raw: Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)

problems.question_html: \(f(x) = x^2 - 5\). Show that \(f\) has a root in \([2, 3]\). What are the values of \(f(2)\) and \(f(3)\)?

hints.text: \(f(2) = -1 < 0\) and \(f(3) = 4 > 0\). Since they have opposite signs, IVT guarantees a root.

solution_steps.text: \(f(2) < 0 < f(3)\), and \(f\) is continuous (polynomial). By IVT, there exists \(c \in (2,3)\) with \(f(c) = 0\).
(We know this root is \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\), but IVT doesn't tell us the exact value.)

problems.question_html: \(f\) is continuous on \([1, 5]\) with \(f(1) = 3\) and \(f(5) = 11\). Must there exist \(c \in (1, 5)\) with \(f(c) = 7\)?

hints.text: Is 7 between \(f(1) = 3\) and \(f(5) = 11\)?
Yes, \(3 < 7 < 11\). Since \(f\) is continuous on \([1,5]\), IVT applies.

problems.question_html: Can IVT guarantee a root of \(g(x) = x^2 + 1\) in \([-1, 1]\)?

hints.text: Compute \(g(-1)\) and \(g(1)\). Do they have opposite signs?
\(g(-1) = 2 > 0\) and \(g(1) = 2 > 0\). Both positive — IVT cannot guarantee a root.

solution_steps.text: IVT cannot guarantee a root because \(N = 0\) is not between \(g(-1) = 2\) and \(g(1) = 2\).
In fact, \(x^2 + 1 > 0\) for all real \(x\) — it has no real roots at all.

problems.question_html: Why does IVT fail for the function \(f(x) = \begin{cases} -1 & x < 0 \\ 1 & x \ge 0 \end{cases}\) on \([-1, 1]\), even though \(f(-1) = -1\) and \(f(1) = 1\) have opposite signs?

hints.text: What is the key hypothesis of IVT?
IVT requires continuity on the closed interval. This function has a jump discontinuity at \(x = 0\).

solution_steps.text: IVT requires \(f\) to be continuous on \([a, b]\). This function jumps from \(-1\) to \(1\) at \(x = 0\).
There is no \(c\) where \(f(c) = 0\) — the function skips the value 0 entirely.
This shows why the continuity hypothesis is essential: without it, IVT's conclusion can fail.

problems.question_html: The function \(f\) is continuous on \([1, 5]\) with \(f(1) = -3\) and \(f(5) = 7\). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, which value must \(f\) take on the interval \((1, 5)\)?

choices.text: The IVT does not guarantee any particular value

hints.text: The IVT says every value between \(f(1)\) and \(f(5)\)  --  that is, between \(-3\) and \(7\)  --  must be achieved.
\(0\) is between \(-3\) and \(7\), so there exists some \(c \in (1, 5)\) with \(f(c) = 0\). The values \(-5\) and \(10\) are outside this range.

solution_steps.text: The IVT guarantees that every value between \(-3\) and \(7\) is achieved by \(f\) on \((1, 5)\).
\(0\) is between \(-3\) and \(7\), so there exists \(c \in (1, 5)\) with \(f(c) = 0\). This also proves \(f\) has at least one root on \((1, 5)\).

problems.question_html: A student claims: "Since \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) satisfies \(f(-1) = -1 < 0\) and \(f(1) = 1 > 0\), the IVT guarantees a root in \((-1, 1)\)." What is wrong with this argument?

choices.text: The function is not continuous on \([-1, 1]\)
The IVT only applies to polynomials

hints.text: The IVT requires continuity on the entire closed interval \([a, b]\).
\(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) is not defined (and not continuous) at \(x = 0\), which is inside \([-1, 1]\). The IVT does not apply.

solution_steps.text: The IVT requires \(f\) to be continuous on the entire closed interval \([-1, 1]\).
\(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) is undefined at \(x = 0\), so it is not continuous on \([-1, 1]\).
Since the hypothesis of the IVT fails, no conclusion can be drawn. Indeed, \(\frac{1}{x} = 0\) has no solution, so the function has no root at all.

problems.question_html:
Show that the equation \(x^3 + x - 1 = 0\) has at least one solution in the interval \((0, 1)\).

(a) Define a function \(f(x)\) and verify the hypotheses of the IVT.

(b) State the conclusion of the IVT as applied to this problem.
problems.sample_answer: Let f(x) = x^3 + x - 1. f is a polynomial, hence continuous on [0,1]. f(0) = -1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0. Since 0 is between -1 and 1, the IVT guarantees a c in (0,1) with f(c) = 0.
rubric: Defines f(x) = x^3 + x - 1 and states it is continuous (polynomial)
Computes f(0) = -1 and f(1) = 1 with correct signs
Applies the IVT to conclude there exists c in (0,1) with f(c) = 0

hints.text: Let \(f(x) = x^3 + x - 1\). Check that \(f\) is continuous and that \(f(0)\) and \(f(1)\) have opposite signs.
\(f(0) = -1 < 0\), \(f(1) = 1 > 0\). Since \(f\) is continuous and changes sign, the IVT guarantees a zero.

solution_steps.text: (a) Let \(f(x) = x^3 + x - 1\). Since \(f\) is a polynomial, it is continuous on \([0, 1]\) (and everywhere).

(b) Since \(f\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\), \(f(0) = -1 < 0 < 1 = f(1)\), the IVT guarantees there exists at least one \(c \in (0, 1)\) such that \(f(c) = 0\). Therefore \(x^3 + x - 1 = 0\) has at least one solution in \((0, 1)\).

problems.correct_answer: Let f(x) = x^3 + x - 1. f is a polynomial, hence continuous on [0,1]. f(0) = -1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0. Since 0 is between -1 and 1, the IVT guarantees a c in (0,1) with f(c) = 0.

problems.question_html:
A continuous function \(f\) on \([0, 4]\) has the values \(f(0) = 2\), \(f(1) = -1\), \(f(2) = 3\), \(f(3) = -2\), \(f(4) = 1\).

(a) What is the minimum number of zeros of \(f\) on \([0, 4]\)?

(b) Identify the intervals in which zeros must occur. Justify using the IVT.
rubric: Identifies all four sign changes between consecutive values
Applies the IVT to each subinterval where a sign change occurs
Correctly concludes the minimum number of zeros is 4

hints.text: The IVT guarantees a zero between any two points where \(f\) changes sign.
Check each consecutive pair: \(f(0) > 0\), \(f(1) < 0\) (sign change); \(f(1) < 0\), \(f(2) > 0\) (sign change); etc.

solution_steps.text: Sign changes between consecutive points: \(f(0) = 2 > 0\) and \(f(1) = -1 < 0\): sign change on \([0, 1]\).
By the IVT (\(f\) is continuous and changes sign), there is at least one zero in each of \((0,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,3)\), and \((3,4)\). The minimum number of zeros is 4.

concepts.title: Defining Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change at a Point
concepts.content_html:
From Average to Instantaneous

In Unit 1, we saw that the limit concept lets us describe what happens at an instant. Now we make this precise for rates of change.

Average Rate of Change

The average rate of change of \(f\) on \([a, b]\) is the slope of the secant line through \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\):

\[\text{AROC} = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\]

Instantaneous Rate of Change

The instantaneous rate of change of \(f\) at \(x = a\) is the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to zero:

\[\text{IROC at } x = a = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\]

Equivalently: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}\)

This is the slope of the tangent line to the graph at \(x = a\).

Key Connection: The instantaneous rate of change at a point is the limit of average rates of change over shorter and shorter intervals. Geometrically, secant lines approach the tangent line.

Example

Find the instantaneous rate of change of \(f(x) = x^2\) at \(x = 3\):

\[\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(3+h)^2 - 9}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{9 + 6h + h^2 - 9}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{6h + h^2}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}(6 + h) = 6\]
concepts.content_raw: Defining Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change at a Point

problem_sets.title: Practice: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change

problems.question_html: What is the average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^3\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 3\)?
Find the instantaneous rate of change of \(f(x) = x^2\) at \(x = 5\) using the limit definition.

hints.text: Compute \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(5+h)^2 - 25}{h}\).

problems.question_html: Find the instantaneous rate of change of \(f(x) = 3x + 7\) at \(x = 2\).

hints.text: For a linear function \(f(x) = mx + b\), the instantaneous rate of change everywhere is the slope \(m\).
The slope is 3.

solution_steps.text: For any linear function, the instantaneous rate of change equals the slope.

problems.question_html: Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{x^2 - 16}{x - 4}\). What does this represent geometrically for \(f(x) = x^2\)?

hints.text: This is the alternative form of the derivative definition: \(\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\) with \(a = 4\).
\(\frac{(x-4)(x+4)}{x-4} = x + 4 \to 8\). This is the slope of the tangent line to \(y = x^2\) at \(x = 4\).

solution_steps.text: This is the instantaneous rate of change (derivative) of \(f(x) = x^2\) at \(x = 4\), i.e., the slope of the tangent line at that point.

problems.question_html: The position of a particle at time \(t\) is given by \(s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t\). What is the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 2\)?

hints.text: The instantaneous velocity is \(s'(t)\). Find the derivative first.
\(s'(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9\). Now evaluate at \(t = 2\).

problems.question_html: For \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\), which expression represents the instantaneous rate of change at \(x = 4\)?

hints.text: The IROC at \(x = a\) uses the limit definition: \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\).
Here \(a = 4\) and \(f(4) = \sqrt{4} = 2\), so the expression is \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{4+h} - 2}{h}\).

solution_steps.text: The instantaneous rate of change at \(x = a\) is \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\).

problems.question_html:
A rock is thrown upward from a bridge. Its height in meters after \(t\) seconds is \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 25\).

(a) Find the average velocity from \(t = 1\) to \(t = 3\).

(b) Use the limit definition to find the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 1\).

(c) At what time does the rock reach its maximum height? Justify your answer using the instantaneous rate of change.
problems.sample_answer:
(a) Average velocity = [h(3) - h(1)] / (3 - 1) = [(-5·9 + 60 + 25) - (-5 + 20 + 25)] / 2 = (40 - 40) / 2 = 0 m/s.
(b) v(1) = lim_{h→0} [h(1+h) - h(1)] / h = lim_{h→0} [-5(1+h)² + 20(1+h) + 25 - 40] / h = lim_{h→0} [-5 - 10h - 5h² + 20 + 20h + 25 - 40] / h = lim_{h→0} [10h - 5h²] / h = lim_{h→0} (10 - 5h) = 10 m/s.
(c) Maximum height occurs when the instantaneous velocity equals zero. h'(t) = -10t + 20 = 0 gives t = 2 seconds. Since h'(t) changes from positive to negative at t = 2, this is a maximum.

(b) Sets up the limit definition correctly and simplifies to get v(1) = 10 m/s
(c) Sets h'(t) = 0, solves t = 2, and justifies it is a maximum

problems.question_html:
The temperature of a cup of coffee \(t\) minutes after being poured is modeled by \(T(t) = 70 + 130e^{-0.04t}\) (in °F).

(a) Find the average rate of change of temperature from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 10\). Include units.

(b) Explain in context what the sign of the average rate of change tells you.

(c) Would you expect the instantaneous rate of change at \(t = 0\) to be greater than or less than the average rate you found in (a)? Justify your reasoning.
problems.sample_answer:
(a) T(0) = 70 + 130 = 200°F. T(10) = 70 + 130e^{-0.4} ≈ 70 + 130(0.6703) ≈ 157.14°F. AROC = (157.14 - 200) / 10 ≈ -4.29 °F/min.
(b) The negative sign means the coffee is cooling down over the interval from 0 to 10 minutes.
(c) The IROC at t = 0 should be more negative (less than) the AROC. At t = 0 the coffee is hottest so it cools fastest. As time passes the rate of cooling slows (the curve is concave up), so the AROC over [0,10] is less steep than the tangent at t = 0.
rubric: (a) Correctly evaluates T(0) = 200 and T(10) ≈ 157.14, computes AROC ≈ -4.29 °F/min with units
(b) Interprets the negative sign as the coffee cooling over time
(c) Correctly argues IROC at t = 0 is more negative than AROC, with concavity or cooling-rate reasoning

For part (c), think about whether the function is concave up or concave down. An exponential decay function cools fastest at the beginning.

(c) The IROC at \(t = 0\) is more negative (steeper decline). Since \(T(t)\) is concave up (exponential decay), the tangent line at \(t = 0\) is steeper than the secant over \([0, 10]\).

concepts.title: Defining the Derivative of a Function and Using Derivative Notation
concepts.content_html:
The Derivative

The derivative of \(f\) at \(x = a\) is defined as:

\[f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\]

provided this limit exists. If it does, we say \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\).

The Derivative as a Function

Replace \(a\) with a variable \(x\) to get the derivative function:

\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}\]

This gives us a new function \(f'(x)\) that tells us the slope of \(f\) at every point.

Notation

There are several notations for the derivative -- they all mean the same thing:

NotationRead as
\(f'(x)\)"f prime of x"
\(\frac{dy}{dx}\)"dy dx" or "the derivative of y with respect to x"
\(\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)]\)"d dx of f of x"
\(y'\)"y prime"
\(\dot{y}\)"y dot" (used in physics for time derivatives)
Key Idea: The derivative \(f'(a)\) gives:
• The slope of the tangent line to \(y = f(x)\) at \(x = a\)
• The instantaneous rate of change of \(f\) at \(x = a\)

Example: Using the Definition

Find \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = x^3\):

\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}(3x^2 + 3xh + h^2) = 3x^2\]
concepts.content_raw: Defining the Derivative of a Function and Using Derivative Notation

problems.question_html: Using the limit definition, find \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = 5x - 2\).

hints.text: \(= \frac{5h}{h} = 5\). The derivative of a linear function is its slope.

problems.question_html: The expression \(\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{9+h} - 3}{h}\) represents the derivative of what function at what point?

hints.text: Match the form \(\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\). Here \(f(a+h) = \sqrt{9+h}\) and \(f(a) = 3 = \sqrt{9}\).
So \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and \(a = 9\).

problems.question_html: Using the limit definition, find \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\).

hints.text: \(\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} = \frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}\). Find a common denominator in the numerator.
\(= \frac{x-(x+h)}{hx(x+h)} = \frac{-h}{hx(x+h)} = \frac{-1}{x(x+h)}\). Now take the limit.

problems.question_html: Which notation represents \(f'(x)\)?

hints.text: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is Leibniz notation for the derivative. \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\) is a difference quotient (not a limit).

solution_steps.text: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is equivalent to \(f'(x)\) when \(y = f(x)\). Both represent the derivative.
\(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\) is the average rate of change (no limit). \(\int\) is integration. \(f^{-1}\) is the inverse.

problems.question_html: Using the limit definition of the derivative, what is \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = 3x^2 - 2x + 1\)?

hints.text: Use \(f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\). Expand \(f(x+h)\) carefully.
\(f(x+h) = 3(x+h)^2 - 2(x+h) + 1 = 3x^2 + 6xh + 3h^2 - 2x - 2h + 1\). Subtract \(f(x)\) and divide by \(h\).

problems.question_html: If \(y = x^3\), which of the following correctly represents \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) using the limit definition?

hints.text: The limit definition is \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\).
With \(f(x) = x^3\), substitute directly: \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h}\). The limit is essential  --  without it, it's just a difference quotient.

solution_steps.text: The derivative is defined as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\).
For \(y = x^3\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h}\). The limit must be present and the subtraction must be \(f(x+h) - f(x)\), not reversed.

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\).

(a) Use the limit definition of the derivative to find \(f'(x)\). Show all algebraic steps.

(b) Evaluate \(f'(3)\) and interpret it as a rate of change.

(c) Write the equation of the tangent line to \(f\) at \(x = 3\).
problems.sample_answer:
(a) f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [1/(x+h) - 1/x] / h = lim_{h→0} [x - (x+h)] / [hx(x+h)] = lim_{h→0} -h / [hx(x+h)] = lim_{h→0} -1 / [x(x+h)] = -1/x².
(b) f'(3) = -1/9. At x = 3, the function is decreasing at a rate of 1/9 unit per unit increase in x.
(c) f(3) = 1/3. Tangent line: y - 1/3 = -1/9(x - 3), or y = -x/9 + 2/3.
rubric: (a) Correctly sets up the limit definition, combines fractions, cancels h, and obtains f'(x) = -1/x²
(b) Evaluates f'(3) = -1/9 and provides a contextual interpretation
(c) Uses point-slope form with (3, 1/3) and slope -1/9 to write the tangent line equation

hints.text: For part (a), combine \(\frac{1}{x+h} - \frac{1}{x}\) into a single fraction using a common denominator of \(x(x+h)\).
After combining: \(\frac{x - (x+h)}{hx(x+h)} = \frac{-h}{hx(x+h)}\). Cancel the \(h\) and take the limit.

solution_steps.text: (b) \(f'(3) = -\frac{1}{9}\). The function is decreasing at \(x = 3\) at a rate of \(\frac{1}{9}\) unit per unit.

(a) f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [1/(x+h) - 1/x] / h = lim_{h→0} [x - (x+h)] / [hx(x+h)] = lim_{h→0} -h / [hx(x+h)] = lim_{h→0} -1 / [x(x+h)] = -1/x².
(b) f'(3) = -1/9. At x = 3, the function is decreasing at a rate of 1/9 unit per unit increase in x.
(c) f(3) = 1/3. Tangent line: y - 1/3 = -1/9(x - 3), or y = -x/9 + 2/3.

problems.question_html:
Consider \(g(x) = \sqrt{2x + 1}\).

(a) Use the limit definition to find \(g'(x)\). (Hint: rationalize the numerator.)

(b) Verify your answer by computing \(g'(0)\) and \(g'(4)\).

(c) For what values of \(x\) is \(g'(x)\) defined? Compare this to the domain of \(g(x)\).
problems.sample_answer:
(a) g'(x) = lim_{h→0} [√(2(x+h)+1) - √(2x+1)] / h. Rationalize: multiply by [√(2x+2h+1) + √(2x+1)] / [√(2x+2h+1) + √(2x+1)]. Numerator becomes (2x+2h+1) - (2x+1) = 2h. So g'(x) = lim_{h→0} 2h / [h(√(2x+2h+1) + √(2x+1))] = 2 / [2√(2x+1)] = 1/√(2x+1).
(b) g'(0) = 1/√1 = 1. g'(4) = 1/√9 = 1/3.
(c) g'(x) = 1/√(2x+1) is defined when 2x + 1 > 0, i.e., x > -1/2. The domain of g is x ≥ -1/2. The derivative is defined on the open interval x > -1/2 (the endpoint x = -1/2 has a vertical tangent).
rubric: (a) Correctly rationalizes the numerator, simplifies to 2h, cancels h, and obtains g'(x) = 1/√(2x+1)
(b) Correctly evaluates g'(0) = 1 and g'(4) = 1/3
(c) States g'(x) requires x > -1/2 (strict), domain of g is x ≥ -1/2, and explains the endpoint

After rationalizing, the numerator simplifies to \(2h\). Cancel \(h\) and take the limit as \(h \to 0\).

(b) g'(0) = 1/√1 = 1. g'(4) = 1/√9 = 1/3.

concepts.title: Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point
concepts.content_html:
Estimating Derivatives

Sometimes we don't have a formula for \(f(x)\) -- we only have a graph or a table. We can still estimate the derivative using nearby values.

From a Table

If you have values of \(f\) at points near \(a\), estimate \(f'(a)\) using the difference quotient over a small interval:

\[f'(a) \approx \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\]

For better accuracy, use the symmetric difference quotient:

\[f'(a) \approx \frac{f(a + h) - f(a - h)}{2h}\]

This averages the slopes from both sides and gives a better estimate.

From a Graph

To estimate \(f'(a)\) from a graph:

  1. Draw (or imagine) the tangent line at \(x = a\)
  2. Pick two points on the tangent line that are easy to read
  3. Compute the slope: \(\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}\)
AP Exam Tip: When estimating a derivative from a table, use the closest available values on either side of the point. If values on only one side are available, use a one-sided difference quotient. Always show your setup (which values you're using and the formula).

problems.question_html:
Given the table:

\(x\)3456
\(f(x)\)10172637

Estimate \(f'(4)\) using the symmetric difference quotient.

hints.text: Symmetric difference quotient: \(\frac{f(5) - f(3)}{5 - 3}\).

problems.question_html: A tangent line to \(y = f(x)\) at \(x = 3\) passes through the points \((1, 2)\) and \((5, 10)\). What is \(f'(3)\)?

hints.text: The derivative at a point equals the slope of the tangent line at that point.

solution_steps.text: The tangent line passes through \((1,2)\) and \((5,10)\).
Slope \(= \frac{10-2}{5-1} = 2\). Since the tangent line's slope equals \(f'(3)\), we have \(f'(3) = 2\).

problems.question_html: Why is the symmetric difference quotient \(\frac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}\) generally a better estimate of \(f'(a)\) than \(\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\)?
problems.correct_answer: it averages both sides||uses both sides||averages slopes from both directions

hints.text: Think about which slopes you're averaging  --  one from the left and one from the right.
The symmetric form averages the forward and backward difference quotients, reducing bias from curvature.

solution_steps.text: The symmetric difference quotient uses information from both sides of \(a\), averaging the forward slope \(\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\) and backward slope \(\frac{f(a)-f(a-h)}{h}\).
This cancels out some of the error due to curvature, giving a more accurate estimate.

problems.question_html:
The table shows values of a differentiable function \(f\).

\(x\)2.02.12.22.3
\(f(x)\)5.005.215.445.69

Using the symmetric difference quotient, which is the best estimate of \(f'(2.1)\)?

hints.text: The symmetric (central) difference quotient uses the points on both sides: \(\frac{f(2.2) - f(2.0)}{2.2 - 2.0}\).

solution_steps.text: The symmetric difference quotient for \(f'(2.1)\) is \(\frac{f(2.2) - f(2.0)}{2.2 - 2.0}\).

problems.question_html: A student estimates \(f'(5)\) using \(\frac{f(5) - f(4)}{5 - 4}\) and gets 3.2, while using \(\frac{f(6) - f(5)}{6 - 5}\) gives 3.8. Using the average of these two estimates, what is the best estimate of \(f'(5)\)?

hints.text: Averaging the left and right difference quotients is equivalent to the symmetric difference quotient.

solution_steps.text: Average the left-hand and right-hand estimates: \(\frac{3.2 + 3.8}{2} = 3.5\).
This equals the symmetric difference quotient \(\frac{f(6) - f(4)}{6 - 4}\), generally the best estimate from table data.

problems.question_html:
The table gives selected values of a twice-differentiable function \(g\).

\(x\)013610
\(g(x)\)47112036

(a) Estimate \(g'(3)\) using the secant line from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 6\). Show your work.

(b) Is your estimate in (a) likely an overestimate or underestimate of the true value? Justify using the data.

(c) Estimate \(g'(6)\) using the symmetric difference quotient with the nearest available data points.
problems.sample_answer:
(a) g'(3) ≈ [g(6) - g(1)] / (6 - 1) = (20 - 7) / 5 = 13/5 = 2.6.
(b) Checking the slopes on sub-intervals: (7-4)/1 = 3, (11-7)/2 = 2, (20-11)/3 = 3, (36-20)/4 = 4. The slopes are increasing (after the initial dip), suggesting g is concave up near x = 3. (c) Nearest points on each side of x = 6 are x = 3 and x = 10. g'(6) ≈ (36 - 11) / (10 - 3) = 25/7 ≈ 3.57.

For a concave up function, the secant line slope over a wide interval may overestimate the derivative at the left portion and underestimate at the right portion. Since 3 is to the left of the midpoint of [1,6], this is likely an overestimate.

concepts.title: Connecting Differentiability and Continuity
concepts.content_html:
Differentiability and Continuity

There is a fundamental connection between differentiability and continuity:

Theorem: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\).

Contrapositive: If \(f\) is not continuous at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = a\).

Warning: The converse is FALSE! Continuity does NOT guarantee differentiability.

When Differentiability Fails

A function can be continuous but not differentiable at a point. This happens at:

  • Corners (cusps): The graph makes a sharp turn. Example: \(f(x) = |x|\) at \(x = 0\). Left-hand derivative = \(-1\), right-hand derivative = \(+1\).
  • Vertical tangent lines: The tangent line is vertical (infinite slope). Example: \(f(x) = x^{1/3}\) at \(x = 0\).

Checking Differentiability at a Point

\(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\) if and only if:

  1. \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\)
  2. \(\displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\) (both one-sided derivatives exist and are equal)

problems.question_html: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = 5\), which of the following must be true?

hints.text: Differentiability at a point implies continuity at that point.
It does NOT tell us the value of \(f'(5)\), the value \(f(5)\), or anything about other points.

solution_steps.text: Differentiability implies continuity. If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = 5\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 5\).

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = |x - 3|\) is continuous at \(x = 3\) but not differentiable there. Why?

choices.text: The function has a vertical asymptote

hints.text: \(|x-3|\) has a V-shape with vertex at \(x = 3\). What happens to the slope?
Left of 3: slope = \(-1\). Right of 3: slope = \(+1\). The one-sided derivatives don't match.

solution_steps.text: Since \(-1 \neq 1\), the derivative doesn't exist at \(x = 3\). The graph has a corner.

problems.question_html: True or false: If \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\).

hints.text: Think of counterexamples: \(|x|\) at \(x = 0\).
\(|x|\) is continuous at 0 but has a corner (not differentiable). Continuity does NOT imply differentiability.

solution_steps.text: False. The converse of 'differentiable implies continuous' is not true.
Counterexample: \(f(x) = |x|\) is continuous at \(x = 0\) but not differentiable there (corner).

problems.question_html: At how many points is \(f(x) = |x^2 - 4|\) not differentiable?

hints.text: \(|x^2-4| = 0\) when \(x^2 - 4 = 0\), i.e., at \(x = \pm 2\). These are where the absolute value creates corners.
The graph of \(x^2-4\) is a parabola opening up. The absolute value flips the part below the \(x\)-axis, creating corners at \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\).

solution_steps.text: \(x^2 - 4 = 0\) at \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\). At these points, \(x^2-4\) changes sign.
The absolute value creates corners at both points, so \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\). That's 2 points.

problems.question_html: The function \(f(x) = |x - 2|\) is:

hints.text: Absolute value functions have a corner (sharp turn) at the vertex. Is the graph continuous there?
The left-hand derivative is \(-1\) and the right-hand derivative is \(+1\). Since they differ, \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 2\), but the function is still continuous.

solution_steps.text: \(f(x) = |x-2|\) has a corner at \(x = 2\). The function is continuous there since \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 0 = f(2)\).
Left derivative: \(\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|h|}{h} = -1\). Right derivative: \(+1\). Since they differ, \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 2\).

problems.question_html: Which statement is always true?

choices.text: If \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\)
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\)
If \(f\) is not continuous at \(x = a\), then \(f\) might still be differentiable at \(x = a\)
If \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is not continuous at \(x = a\)

hints.text: Remember the theorem: differentiability implies continuity. Does the converse hold?
Differentiable \(\Rightarrow\) continuous is always true. Continuous \(\not\Rightarrow\) differentiable (counterexample: \(|x|\) at 0).

solution_steps.text: The theorem states: if \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = a\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(x = a\).
The converse is false: \(f(x) = |x|\) is continuous at \(x = 0\) but not differentiable there (corner).

problems.question_html:
Consider the piecewise function:

\[f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 \sin\!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) & x \neq 0 \\ 0 & x = 0 \end{cases}\]

(a) Show that \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).

(b) Use the limit definition to determine whether \(f\) is differentiable at \(x = 0\). If so, find \(f'(0)\).

(c) Is \(f'\) continuous at \(x = 0\)? Explain why or why not.
problems.sample_answer:
(a) |f(x)| = |x² sin(1/x)| ≤ x² for all x ≠ 0. Since lim_{x→0} x² = 0 = f(0), by the Squeeze Theorem, f is continuous at x = 0.
(b) f'(0) = lim_{h→0} [f(h) - f(0)] / h = lim_{h→0} h² sin(1/h) / h = lim_{h→0} h sin(1/h) = 0 (by Squeeze Theorem since |h sin(1/h)| ≤ |h|). So f'(0) = 0.
(c) For x ≠ 0, f'(x) = 2x sin(1/x) - cos(1/x) by the product and chain rules. As x → 0, cos(1/x) oscillates between -1 and 1 and does not have a limit. Therefore f' is not continuous at x = 0.
rubric: (a) Uses the Squeeze Theorem with -x² ≤ f(x) ≤ x² to show continuity at x = 0
(b) Correctly applies the limit definition and Squeeze Theorem to find f'(0) = 0
(c) Computes f'(x) for x ≠ 0 and shows cos(1/x) has no limit as x → 0, so f' is not continuous

hints.text: For part (a), use the Squeeze Theorem: \(-x^2 \leq x^2 \sin(1/x) \leq x^2\).
For part (b), \(\frac{f(h) - 0}{h} = h\sin(1/h)\). Apply the Squeeze Theorem again with \(-|h| \leq h\sin(1/h) \leq |h|\).

solution_steps.text: (a) \(|x^2 \sin(1/x)| \leq x^2 \to 0\). By the Squeeze Theorem, \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0 = f(0)\), so \(f\) is continuous.
(c) For \(x \neq 0\): \(f'(x) = 2x\sin(1/x) - \cos(1/x)\). The \(\cos(1/x)\) term oscillates and has no limit as \(x \to 0\), so \(f'\) is not continuous at 0.

problems.correct_answer:
(a) |f(x)| = |x² sin(1/x)| ≤ x² for all x ≠ 0. Since lim_{x→0} x² = 0 = f(0), by the Squeeze Theorem, f is continuous at x = 0.
(b) f'(0) = lim_{h→0} [f(h) - f(0)] / h = lim_{h→0} h² sin(1/h) / h = lim_{h→0} h sin(1/h) = 0 (by Squeeze Theorem since |h sin(1/h)| ≤ |h|). So f'(0) = 0.
(c) For x ≠ 0, f'(x) = 2x sin(1/x) - cos(1/x) by the product and chain rules. As x → 0, cos(1/x) oscillates between -1 and 1 and does not have a limit. Therefore f' is not continuous at x = 0.

problems.question_html:
Define

\[g(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + 1 & x \leq 1 \\ 2x + c & x > 1 \end{cases}\]

(a) Find the value of \(c\) that makes \(g\) continuous at \(x = 1\).

(b) With that value of \(c\), determine whether \(g\) is differentiable at \(x = 1\). Justify using left-hand and right-hand derivatives.

(c) Sketch the graph of \(g\) near \(x = 1\) and describe what you observe geometrically.
problems.sample_answer:
(a) For continuity: lim_{x→1⁻} g(x) = 1² + 1 = 2. lim_{x→1⁺} g(x) = 2(1) + c = 2 + c. Set equal: 2 + c = 2, so c = 0.
(b) Left derivative: lim_{h→0⁻} [g(1+h) - g(1)] / h = lim_{h→0⁻} [(1+h)² + 1 - 2] / h = lim_{h→0⁻} [2h + h²] / h = lim_{h→0⁻} (2 + h) = 2. Right derivative: lim_{h→0⁺} [2(1+h) - 2] / h = lim_{h→0⁺} 2h / h = 2. Since both one-sided derivatives equal 2, g is differentiable at x = 1.
(c) The graph shows a parabola for x ≤ 1 and a line for x > 1. At x = 1, the pieces join smoothly (no corner) because both the function values and slopes match.
rubric: (a) Sets left and right limits equal and solves c = 0
(b) Computes both one-sided derivatives as 2 and concludes g is differentiable
(c) Describes smooth join (no corner/cusp) with matching slopes

hints.text: For continuity, the left-hand limit \(\lim_{x \to 1^-} g(x)\) must equal the right-hand limit \(\lim_{x \to 1^+} g(x) = g(1)\).
For differentiability, compute the left-hand derivative \((g(1+h) - g(1))/h\) as \(h \to 0^-\) using the \(x^2+1\) piece, and the right-hand derivative using the \(2x\) piece.

solution_steps.text: (a) Left limit: \(1^2 + 1 = 2\). Right limit: \(2(1) + c = 2 + c\). Set equal: \(c = 0\).
(b) Left derivative: \(\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{(1+h)^2 + 1 - 2}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-}(2 + h) = 2\). Right derivative: \(\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{2(1+h) - 2}{h} = 2\). Equal, so \(g\) is differentiable.
(c) The parabola and line meet at \((1, 2)\) with the same slope of 2, creating a smooth transition with no corner.

problems.correct_answer:
(a) For continuity: lim_{x→1⁻} g(x) = 1² + 1 = 2. lim_{x→1⁺} g(x) = 2(1) + c = 2 + c. Set equal: 2 + c = 2, so c = 0.
(b) Left derivative: lim_{h→0⁻} [g(1+h) - g(1)] / h = lim_{h→0⁻} [(1+h)² + 1 - 2] / h = lim_{h→0⁻} [2h + h²] / h = lim_{h→0⁻} (2 + h) = 2. Right derivative: lim_{h→0⁺} [2(1+h) - 2] / h = lim_{h→0⁺} 2h / h = 2. Since both one-sided derivatives equal 2, g is differentiable at x = 1.
(c) The graph shows a parabola for x ≤ 1 and a line for x > 1. At x = 1, the pieces join smoothly (no corner) because both the function values and slopes match.

concepts.title: Applying the Power Rule
concepts.content_html:
The Power Rule

The limit definition works but is tedious. The Power Rule gives us a shortcut for differentiating powers of \(x\):

Power Rule: If \(f(x) = x^n\), then \(f'(x) = nx^{n-1}\)

This works for any real number \(n\): integers, fractions, negatives.

Examples

  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[x^5] = 5x^4\)
  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[x^{-2}] = -2x^{-3} = \frac{-2}{x^3}\)
  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[\sqrt{x}] = \frac{d}{dx}[x^{1/2}] = \frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\)
  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[x^{2/3}] = \frac{2}{3}x^{-1/3}\)

Special Cases

  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[x] = 1\) (since \(x = x^1\), so \(1 \cdot x^0 = 1\))
  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[c] = 0\) for any constant \(c\) (constants have zero rate of change)

Rewriting Before Differentiating

Always rewrite roots and fractions as powers before applying the rule:

  • \(\sqrt[3]{x} = x^{1/3}\)
  • \(\frac{1}{x^4} = x^{-4}\)
  • \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2}\)

problems.question_html:
Let \(f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2 + 16\).

(a) Find \(f'(x)\) using the power rule.

(b) Find all values of \(x\) where \(f'(x) = 0\).

(c) Factor \(f(x)\) and explain geometrically what happens at the zeros of \(f'\).
problems.sample_answer:
(a) f'(x) = 4x³ - 16x.
(b) 4x³ - 16x = 0 → 4x(x² - 4) = 0 → 4x(x-2)(x+2) = 0 → x = 0, x = 2, x = -2.
(c) f(x) = (x² - 4)². The function has a double root at x = ±2 (touches the x-axis) and a local maximum at x = 0. The zeros of f' are where the tangent line is horizontal: local max at x = 0, local minima at x = ±2.
rubric: (a) Correctly applies the power rule to get f'(x) = 4x³ - 16x
(b) Factors and solves to get x = 0, 2, -2
(c) Factors f(x) = (x²-4)² and describes the geometric meaning of horizontal tangent lines

hints.text: For part (a), apply the power rule term by term: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^4) = 4x^3\), etc.
For part (b), factor out \(4x\) from \(4x^3 - 16x\) to get \(4x(x^2 - 4)\).

solution_steps.text: (c) \(f(x) = (x^2 - 4)^2\). At \(x = \pm 2\), the graph touches the \(x\)-axis (local minima). At \(x = 0\), the graph has a local maximum. These are the points with horizontal tangent lines.

problems.correct_answer:
(a) f'(x) = 4x³ - 16x.
(b) 4x³ - 16x = 0 → 4x(x² - 4) = 0 → 4x(x-2)(x+2) = 0 → x = 0, x = 2, x = -2.
(c) f(x) = (x² - 4)². The function has a double root at x = ±2 (touches the x-axis) and a local maximum at x = 0. The zeros of f' are where the tangent line is horizontal: local max at x = 0, local minima at x = ±2.

(b) Applies power rule to get h'(x) = 5x^{3/2} - (1/2)x^{-1/2}
(c) Evaluates h(1) = 1 and h'(1) = 9/2, writes correct tangent line equation

After simplifying, apply the power rule to each term. Remember \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{5/2}) = \frac{5}{2}x^{3/2}\).

concepts.title: Derivative Rules: Constant, Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple
concepts.content_html:
Basic Derivative Rules

Combined with the Power Rule, these rules let you differentiate any polynomial quickly.

Basic Rules:
1. Constant Rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}[c] = 0\)
2. Constant Multiple Rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}[c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot f'(x)\)
3. Sum Rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}[f(x) + g(x)] = f'(x) + g'(x)\)
4. Difference Rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}[f(x) - g(x)] = f'(x) - g'(x)\)

In Words

Constants factor out of derivatives. Derivatives distribute over addition and subtraction (just like limits do).

Examples

  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[5x^3] = 5 \cdot 3x^2 = 15x^2\)
  • \(\frac{d}{dx}[x^4 - 3x^2 + 7x - 2] = 4x^3 - 6x + 7\)
  • \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{2}{3}x^6 + \sqrt{x}\right] = 4x^5 + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\)

Notice: differentiate each term independently, then combine. You can always break a polynomial into separate terms.
concepts.content_raw: Derivative Rules: Constant, Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple

\(\frac{d}{dx}(\sqrt{2}) = 0\) because \(\sqrt{2}\) is a constant. The derivative of \(\pi x\) is \(\pi\), not \(1\).
Use the constant multiple and difference rules: \(g'(x) = 3f'(x) - 2h'(x)\).

problems.question_html:
A particle moves along a line with position function \(s(t) = 5t^3 - 12t^2 + 9t + 1\) (in meters, \(t\) in seconds).

(a) Find the velocity function \(v(t)\) and the acceleration function \(a(t)\).

(b) Find all times when the particle is at rest.

(c) Find all times when the acceleration is zero. Is the particle speeding up or slowing down at that moment? Justify.
problems.sample_answer:
(a) v(t) = s'(t) = 15t² - 24t + 9. a(t) = v'(t) = 30t - 24.
(b) 15t² - 24t + 9 = 0 → 5t² - 8t + 3 = 0 → (5t - 3)(t - 1) = 0 → t = 3/5 and t = 1.
(c) 30t - 24 = 0 → t = 4/5. v(4/5) = 15(16/25) - 24(4/5) + 9 = 48/5 - 96/5 + 45/5 = -3/5. Since v(4/5) < 0 and a(4/5) = 0, the acceleration is changing sign. Just before t = 4/5, a < 0 and v < 0 (same sign → speeding up). Just after, a > 0 and v < 0 (opposite signs → slowing down). At exactly t = 4/5, the particle is neither speeding up nor slowing down (speed is at a local extreme).
rubric: (a) Correctly differentiates to get v(t) = 15t² - 24t + 9 and a(t) = 30t - 24
(b) Solves the quadratic to get t = 3/5 and t = 1
(c) Finds t = 4/5, evaluates v(4/5), and discusses whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down

hints.text: Velocity is the first derivative of position, and acceleration is the second derivative.
The particle is at rest when \(v(t) = 0\). Factor \(15t^2 - 24t + 9 = 3(5t^2 - 8t + 3) = 3(5t - 3)(t - 1)\).

solution_steps.text: (c) \(a(t) = 0\) at \(t = \frac{4}{5}\). \(v(\tfrac{4}{5}) = -\frac{3}{5} < 0\). Since \(a\) changes from negative to positive while \(v < 0\), the particle transitions from speeding up to slowing down at this instant.

problems.correct_answer:
(a) v(t) = s'(t) = 15t² - 24t + 9. a(t) = v'(t) = 30t - 24.
(b) 15t² - 24t + 9 = 0 → 5t² - 8t + 3 = 0 → (5t - 3)(t - 1) = 0 → t = 3/5 and t = 1.
(c) 30t - 24 = 0 → t = 4/5. v(4/5) = 15(16/25) - 24(4/5) + 9 = 48/5 - 96/5 + 45/5 = -3/5. Since v(4/5) < 0 and a(4/5) = 0, the acceleration is changing sign. Just before t = 4/5, a < 0 and v < 0 (same sign → speeding up). Just after, a > 0 and v < 0 (opposite signs → slowing down). At exactly t = 4/5, the particle is neither speeding up nor slowing down (speed is at a local extreme).

concepts.title: Derivatives of cos x, sin x, e^x, and ln x
concepts.content_html:
Essential Derivative Formulas

Beyond polynomials, you need to know the derivatives of the fundamental transcendental functions:

Must-Know Derivatives:
\(\frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] = \cos x\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = -\sin x\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[e^x] = e^x\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[\ln x] = \frac{1}{x}\) for \(x > 0\)

Why These Matter

  • Sine and cosine are the building blocks for all trig derivatives (tangent, secant, etc. come later via the quotient rule)
  • \(e^x\) is remarkable: it's the only function that is its own derivative. \(\frac{d}{dx}[e^x] = e^x\)
  • \(\ln x\) is the inverse of \(e^x\), and its derivative \(\frac{1}{x}\) will appear constantly in integration

General Exponential

For \(a^x\) where \(a > 0\), \(a \neq 1\):

\[\frac{d}{dx}[a^x] = a^x \ln a\]

When \(a = e\), this simplifies to \(e^x \cdot \ln e = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x\).

General Logarithm

\[\frac{d}{dx}[\log_a x] = \frac{1}{x \ln a}\]

When \(a = e\), this simplifies to \(\frac{1}{x}\).

Combining with Previous Rules

\(\frac{d}{dx}[3\sin x + 2e^x - 5\ln x] = 3\cos x + 2e^x - \frac{5}{x}\)
